utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours and everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Jadranko Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is Tuesday, September 2nd, and first I welcome our witness, the accused, the counsel for Defence, as well as the representatives of the OTP and everyone helping us. We will now continue with the examination-in-chief led by Mr. Karnavas. I remind you all that we will stop at 12.30 and resume at 2.15, not 2.30, 2.15 p.m. Mr. Karnavas, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Perkovic. I trust you had a good night's sleep and are ready to answer more questions today.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's finish off where we were yesterday with respect to the seals. There was a lengthy discussion, far more than I had anticipated, so let's go back to this document of 1D 00014. And I just want to point a couple of things out in light of the questioning yesterday. From Article 1 it says here that the stamp will contain the name of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, hereinafter RBiH, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, HZ HB. Let me stop right there. If we were to look at this, could someone mistake Article 1 as giving HZ HB state-like powers and becoming a statelet or a state of its own? And I'm particularly stressing this point in light of some of the questioning that occurred yesterday.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could not draw that conclusion. All the institutions of power at all levels had names that clearly reflected the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, starting with the municipal authorities and then working your way up all the way to the federal level. The only thing we can conclude on this -- based on this is that this is an organ or institution that has the power to set up certain authorities for certain segments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And of course in Article 2 we can see again they make reference to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But moving on, if we go to Article 10 very briefly, because this will help us in looking at some of the other documents very quickly, Article 10 talks about: "The head of the HVO HZ HB, justice and administration department, shall adopt a separate directive on making, storage, use, and keeping of records ..." Now, in light of this Article let's look at some of the other documents very quickly, 1D 00015, here we have a directive on making storage and usage, usage of keeping of records, and of course if we go to the last page we see Zoran Buntic, and you would confirm that Zoran Buntic at the time was the head of the department of justice, is that correct, justice and administration?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And in Article 1 it talks about as far as the -- authorising a particular manufacturer, it would be up to the department of interior. Do you see that, Article 1, right?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the next document, 1D 00016, here we see a directive on the work of certified manufacturers of stamps, and of course if we go to the last page of this document we see head of department Branko Kvesic, and he was indeed the head of the department of interior, was he not, during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then of course the next document, 1D 00065, we see a decision, and this decision authorises this particular enterprise, Grafotisak, as being the manufacturer of the stamps and of course again we see it is Branko Kvesic who has signed this particular decision. Now, if we go to -- as a way of example because we don't need to go through all the documents, 1D 02126, let's see how this is put into play, that is, getting a stamp. Here we see a request by Dr. Jadranko Prlic and he is submitting a request for permission to make a seal, and of course he designates under 1 and 2, and this is dated 9 September. Just a quick question. I mean, here is Dr. Jadranko Prlic, he's the president, why does he need to make a request? Why can't he use his presidential powers? And I point this out because specifically in this courtroom we've heard testimony that somehow Jadranko Prlic had more powers than anybody else at times, especially when it came to HVO, the executive authority. So why would he need to ask for a request? Why can't he just simply say, Make a -- direct me to the manufacturer and have it done?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order for an institution to get a seal there is a procedure on the making of such seals and stamps and there is the decree on seals. In keeping with that, each head of an institution, including the head of the HVO, must act in keeping with those regulations and in keeping with those regulations they have the right to use a seal. This is a commitment that applies throughout, it applies to everyone. The regulations of the HZ HB made no allowances for anyone, including the president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You need to slow down a little bit to make sure that we get everything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: -- if I may have some further clarification. Witness, the request is to the HZ HB HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The department for justice and administration of the HVO of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And there is reference to Article 3 of the instructions on creating, et cetera, of seals. What kind of a decree is that? Is it one that we have seen here? I'm not quite sure whether I have seen it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The instructions, this is 1D 000016.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. And this decree of course is also a Herceg-Bosna norm, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a norm in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and as such it is accepted there. Up until the war we had enactments like that, especially the instructions on the making of seals, there was a special legal norm governing the making of seals, and there was a special decision on institutions and companies that would be authorised to produce, make, such seals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. It's the usual linguistic system. Here it is referred to instructions and this is called directive, this is a bit confusing, so I'm sorry if I asked a redundant question. But the gist of it, of my question, is that when you say it is the rules it is HV rules, and it's no reference on any rules established by BiH; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So what we have here is three different legal regulations. We have a decree, which is in practical terms an amendment to whatever authorisations in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina were prescribed by law; we have special instructions, this is a sort of bylaw, special form of bylaw, detailing how the seal-makers should work, the institutions producing the seals. This is something that is not unusual because these issues are always settled by a special legal enactment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, obviously my question was not quite clear enough. All the enactments, that is what I would be assured of, are enactments of Herceg-Bosna and there's no reference to any legislation of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Looking at these instructions and the decree on seals or stamps, what you suggest is entirely accurate because in the norms that prevailed in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina one simply couldn't find any foothold for making seals for Herceg-Bosna, simply because Herceg-Bosna was a transitional form of government according to the republican regulations and nothing like this was provided for. In essence, a legal analogy was applied here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From the line of questioning it would appear that what was happening is there was a question as to whether by not making reference to Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the republic, in a sense Herceg-Bosna now is acting as a state. And I mention this in particular because there was a particular expert analyst by the Prosecution who makes, you know, takes this and pigeonholes this into a theory that this is sort of an indication of taking on state-like powers and thereby we can conclude that Herceg-Bosna was a state. Is that what's happening here by not referencing anything to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I can't agree that there is no reference to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in the document. If you go through the decree carefully you see also, when you look at what the substance of the seal should be, there is a prescription to use always the term Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm only talking about the fact that no regulation could be taken over from Bosnia-Herzegovina that would settle this issue simply because Bosnia-Herzegovina had no regulation talking about the seals of Herceg-Bosna. It wasn't that we could apply our usual course of action here, to simply take over laws and regulations from Bosnia-Herzegovina. This was about the procedure of taking over other regulations of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Herceg-Bosna, which doesn't rule out any mention of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in these regulations, and it doesn't mean that the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would not be referred to in any seal or official document of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could -- and then again, in part of your answer we're going to skip one document and then get back to it, but just -- because you talked about controlling. If we look at 1D 00129 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm skipping a document, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: -- this is a directive of keeping a record of and making stamps. And of course this is what you were referring to, that there's sort of a strict control as to keeping a record because of the importance of having a stamp in light of the legal and administrative tradition of Bosnia-Herzegovina; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And then if we go back one document just to see -- I believe one document, 1D 00615, here we see for the Mostar municipality they have enacted a decision on making stamps for business and social organizations in Mostar municipality. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And would it be correct to say that other municipalities, including municipalities that were under the control of the Muslim authorities, were also using stamps in the same fashion?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I guess could we conclude if they were using stamps that perhaps those municipalities under the Muslim authorities were trying somehow to exhibit elements of statehood or para-statehood?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is the same as the one in relation to the previous case. We have a prerequisite for all the organs of government to be functioning and that is the use of a seal, and the seal always contains something that means something else. In this sense, the use of a seal by the municipal authorities in territory controlled by the BH army as well as in Herceg-Bosna means no more than lending legitimacy to these authorities in the sense of there being an authorisation for them to pass appropriate legal enactments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Just one final question and this goes for other issues as well. We heard from an expert by the name of Tomljanovich, they call him an expert on analysis, we'll let the Trial Chamber decide if he is such. In any event, were you ever contacted by Tomljanovich or anybody else from the Office of the Prosecution in light of the fact that you testified in Kordic and obviously that you knew -- they knew who you were and knew what you had done and knew what you had done, did they ever contact you to, for instance, go over some of these things to figure out the practice, the procedure, the culture - and by that I mean the legal culture - in Bosnia-Herzegovina that might have helped them in their assessment? Because it would appear to me that if I'm an expert I would want to seek out somebody like you, and I think Judge Trechsel was quite right in saying that you are a breath of fresh air, having somebody as knowledgeable as you here to talk about these issues. So my question is: Did anybody from the Office of the Prosecution ever contact you in order to figure out some of these issues that we're discussing here today?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no one ever contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And had they contacted you, had they contacted you, would you have made yourself available, as you did with the Prlic Defence, to discuss these issues?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I see no reason not to respond to someone to a request like that. I would be only too glad to provide any explanation that I might be able to offer to either the Defence or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, let's go on to the next document, 1D 00134. This is a decree on employment relations, and of course here we see on Article 1: "The Decree Law of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ... shall be applied ..." we see that in Article 1. And if we look at Article 3, and this might be of some -- I want you to comment on this for a second. It says: "Only fixed-term employment shall be possible ..." If you could explain to us what does that mean: "Only fixed-term employment shall be possible ..."

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina the most frequent situation was this: People would be employed for an indeterminate period of time. The situation we find here is quite the opposite. This is fixed-term employment. A regulation like this was laid down primarily because this was something that was passed after a state of war had been declared, and most of the active population had been sent to the front line while small portions of the active population, as soon as those people had been mobilised and left for the front line, now had an opportunity to take up their jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I may, the legislator is specifying here that this is a temporary situation. If someone is mobilised, if someone is at the front line, that doesn't mean that they would in the future be disadvantaged when applying for a job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But Article 3, granted we know what it was supposed to be and what -- why it was there, was this used for the purposes of denying Muslims or Serbs positions? In other words, was the law drafted in such a way or applied in a way for the specific purpose of denying anyone other than Croats fixed-term employment or unfixed-term employment, I should say, unlimited employment?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No provision of this decree could possibly lead to a conclusion like that. It applies to all of the HZ HB's citizens, all those who lived there. I'm not ruling out the possibility that in individual cases a provision like this could have been misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As is always the case, it's always possible to misuse a certain legal enactment or a law, but that was certainly not the idea behind this nor am I aware of this being any sort of a prominent occurrence at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 02305, 1D 02305, this is a decree on the application of the Law on State Administration in the territory, and we see the word "territory" again, of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna during the state of war or imminent threat of war. I don't want to dwell on whether in the title the word "territory" or "area" is used, but I would like you to focus on Article 3. It says here: "The provisions of the Law on the relations between republican and municipal inspectoral bodies shall also be applied according to the relations between the inspectoral bodies of the HZ HB Croatian Defence Council and the inspectoral bodies of municipal Croatian Defence Councils." Could you please explain what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a republican law specifying in detail what the relationship be between the republican organs of inspection and the municipal organs of inspection in the sense of the powers that the republican organs had vis-a-vis the municipal organs. The belief prevailed that one should not try and re-invent the wheel, but rather to take the solutions that were already there in terms of the relations between the republican organs of inspection and municipal organs of inspection, and to apply these to the relations between the inspection organs of Herceg-Bosna and the municipal inspection organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it, having heard your testimony yesterday, we're talking about pretty much the sort of work that you were doing prior, I believe, to the elections; is that correct? That's the sort of -- what you're referencing to or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let me just --

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a year and a half, nearly two years in fact, I worked as a republican inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And the reason I want to make sure -- now perhaps you can help us here. During this period, in light of Sarajevo being under siege, part of the country being cut off, were the republican inspectoral bodies able to carry out their functions at the municipal level, much like you had been able to do prior to the elections when you were in that position?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 80 per cent of the cases before the war, the republic inspectors acted based on complaints of residents concerning the work of the municipal administration. In wartime when Sarajevo was completely surrounded and it was the seat of the state institutions, I don't see a single possibility for the residents to apply the old system that was used before the war to said complaints on the work of state organs so that certain steps could be taken and illegal conduct reversed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I also understand your position back then, you would on occasion travel to municipalities incognito, as it were, without announcing your presence, and do a spot-check. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in light of that, was that possible during the wartime? In other words, somebody from Sarajevo going to a particular municipality to do to spot-check to see whether the administrative procedures in a particular organ are being adhered to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of inspection organs of the republics acting -- of the republic acting in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to Article 10, because this has been an issue in this court, and it goes to this whole issue of Croatisation, this is one element according to the Prosecution's theory, here we see under Article 10 that there is an introduction of Croatian dinars as a form of payment. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Article 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And please explain to us why -- why were Croatian dinars being introduced as opposed to just dinars? I suspect that if it was just dinars we're talking about Bosnian and Herzegovinian dinars, assuming that they were in existence and had some sort of value.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word "dinar," as used in this article means the former currency of the SFRY, so the former Yugoslav dinar, not the BH dinar. And Croatian dinar was introduced because that currency was the most widely available at that time, both in the hands of citizens and in the hands of institutions. So the most frequent currency for monetary transactions used in actual life during that time was the Croatian dinar. Most likely, if we had as many dollars as we had dinars we would have used dollars.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to 1D 00132, and this is a decree on the implementation on the decree law on the adoption of the Law on General Administration Procedure, and of course we're talking about the RBiH law. If we look at Article 2 it says: "Complaints in the administrative procedure shall be addressed by a second-instance body at the HVO HZ HB ..." If you could please explain to us, why was it necessary to have this particular article?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, if one wishes - and there was this wish to implement the actual supervision and control over the work of the municipal administration, then one could do it in two ways. One was by way of inspection, that kind of supervision, and the other way is by reviewing complaints of citizens on the work of the first-instance organs. This decision, this decree, regulates this, it provides the possibility to use the appeals system, appeals procedure, to reverse, to correct, the administrative acts of municipal administration pursuant to complaints by citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, in light of your previous answers, could you please tell us where the second-instance body would have been. Assuming that there was no war, BiH wasn't occupied, Sarajevo wasn't under siege, where would the second-instance body normally be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are now dealing with the Law on Administrative Procedure of the former SFRY. One of its basic principles was the principle of a two-level procedure, including the appeals instance. This law provided that an enactment of any administrative organ of any sort of authority could be appealed. In most cases, the second-instance body was the republic administration organ located in Sarajevo. However, when that organ decided in the first instance, pursuant to the Law on Administrative Procedure, then the second-instance organ was the relevant organ at the level of the SFRY, that is to say the federal state. It was necessary to ensure that there was a two-level procedure, two-instance procedure, deciding on the appeals and complaints of the citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go to 1D 02011, this is the last document in this chapter, it's a report on the work period of January till June 1993. If we look at the very last page of this document we see your name, Zoran Perkovic, 13 July 1993. And then if we take a glance at the various decrees we see what I suspect had been passed during this period of time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can see here a kind of enactments of the HVO of the HZ HB, and these enactments were submitted for review to the commission which I headed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions, I'll move on to the next topic, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Witness, I have a question, a follow-up question. On the last -- this last document is quite interesting because it gives a review of all the texts that were adopted from June to July 1993, and we see that there are many of them, at least 52 decrees. I followed very carefully all the questions put to you and your answers. We saw that there are some texts that dealt with fixed-term contracts, contrary to nonfixed-term contracts. So I was wondering this: If there was a dispute on the contract, what -- which judge should be seized of it? According to your law, it should be the judge where the person was employed, I guess. But the following question crops up in my mind after this. You say that all these texts were adopted following the failure of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was not able to fulfil its mission and adopt routine acts that would -- needed for the Croats, for example. But why is it that the -- why is it that the administration of Herceg-Bosna did not send to the republic, to Sarajevo, to the competent ministry copy of the document adopted for the -- for their information? What prevented you from sending to the Ministry of Justice, for example, in Sarajevo a copy of the text adopted on the seals? Why -- what prevented you from sending to the labour ministry in Sarajevo a copy of the text adopted on labour laws and contracts? Why didn't you just CC the relevant ministries in Sarajevo? Why didn't you do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that there are several reasons why this was not done. First of all, technically speaking, I don't see how we could have sent this. We could have perhaps taken this by hand to Sarajevo, gone to Sarajevo, and given this to somebody because there was no other means of communicating with Sarajevo. Had we done that, had we used a courier to take this to Sarajevo, I'm not sure how that would have been received in Sarajevo, whether they would have seen this as a provocation or whether they would have seen this as an instance of our sincere desire to inform them of the enactments that we had passed. And additionally, my own experience indicates that they were not interested even in the drafts of the decisions that we deemed important for the entire area. Finally, something very important, we were quite sure that they in Sarajevo had all those regulations and enactments. The fact that in June or July of 1992, what you said yesterday, the constitutional court reviewed basic decisions on the creation of the HZ HB, and that indicated to us that if they had all those enactments then they also had all enactments passed by the HZ HB. And finally, these enactments were no secret. They were published in the Official Gazette of the HZ HB called Narodne Novine, and as such they were available to an indefinite number of people, all those who wanted to acquaint themselves with those texts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: One aspect of your response is somewhat surprising. You say that those in Sarajevo, I put it a bit generally, knew anyway. Well, whether that be so or not, how did you know? We have been told by other witnesses that the HVO was not even aware of the constitutional court's judgement. So you seem to be saying that they knew what documents were before the constitutional court. I find it difficult to reconcile this. Could you perhaps explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, a question was put to me why we hadn't sent these documents to Sarajevo so that the people in Sarajevo who were interested in it would know about this. I in my response said that it was my belief that they knew about these documents. Yesterday I also spoke about diverse and comprehensive and continued contacts that existed between representatives of the institutions of Herceg-Bosna with their colleagues from the republic administration organs in Sarajevo. Based on all that information, I came to the conclusion, or rather, it was my impression that every institution in Sarajevo which wanted to be familiar with the regulations of the HZ HB could familiarize themselves with them without any documents actually being sent there. And as I said, technically it was practically impossible to send them there at that time. When it comes to the enactments of the republic administration organs in Sarajevo and our knowledge of these enactments, I have to say that we were handicapped, those of us who worked in the institutions of the HZ HB, handicapped in that regard. I, for example, knew that the constitutional court passed a decision declaring the HZ HB unconstitutional; however, I had no occasion to review the actual text as a lawyer and analyse it. Simply speaking, one could gain information either by way of people coming out of Sarajevo or by way of listening to radio programme, for example, we could listen to Radio Sarajevo broadcasts; but otherwise there was quite a problem in receiving these enactments of the republic organs in our territory and that problem persisted for quite a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And one follow-up question. Do you know whether other municipalities, like, for instance, Tuzla, was obligated to send its draft legislation or legislation that had been passed to Sarajevo for the Sarajevo authorities to give its blessing?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The enactments of the Tuzla municipal authorities which I had occasion to review indicate that they also had no contact whatsoever with the seat in Sarajevo. Their enactments from the formal, legal point of view have so many unlawful provisions that it is simply improbable that the republic organs would not have reacted and started an initiative to amend those enactments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next chapter now, this deals with minutes more or less, and we're going to go to P 02509 very quickly. And we see in this page, this is the -- we can see that this is from a meeting with the president, Mate Boban, and others. And we see that your name is there, Mr. Zoran Perkovic, and it's under C, the province number 10. Could you please tell us what this is about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are the activities stemming from the desire to implement Vance-Owen Plan. That plan envisioned the creation of provinces in Bosnia and Herzegovina, including provinces number 8, 9, and 10. When it comes to the province number 10, it was proposed for that province that the members of the interim government would be certain people, among whom I was listed as well as a member of that government cabinet. Just to remind you, that was the province whose seat was supposed to be in Travnik, and all the people proposed as potential members of the government in province number 10 were the people who had residence in the territory of that province.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01609, this is dated 26th May 1993. There are all sorts of issues that we can discuss, but I'm only going to focus on one aspect and the Judges may wish to ask questions on this document. But if we look at item number 8 it talks about: "A working group was appointed to visit Central Bosnia comprising of Zuljevic, Perkovic, and if necessary Zubak." Can you tell us what was this about?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, this session was held at a time when there was an escalation of conflicts between Croats and Bosniaks. A working group was designated with a task to go to Central Bosnia and to establish there on the ground the actual situation concerning the daily life in that territory, and then they were supposed to inform the HVO upon their return. There were various contradictory pieces of information coming to us, and they wanted to send a delegation to the area to establish the actual situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And very briefly, did you, in fact, go there to see what was happening over there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't. Our trip was cancelled due to an additional complication, that is to say, the war broke out in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm going to go on to another document unless the Trial Chamber has any questions. Seeing none, we'll go to 1D 01668. These are minutes from 15 June 1993, and of course relevant to the question that I'm going to be asking you -- if we look at the very last paragraph on the first page, we see some remarks by Mr. Kvesic, supporting or upholding the proposal made by Mr. Stojic that the BH army be declared an enemy army and the supreme commander Izetbegovic a war criminal. We see the next page Zubak, who upheld the proposal, but said that he believed that more serious steps should be taken to pull military units out of the areas outside the outlined Croatian provinces, together with the local Croatian inhabitants. And then of course if we look at the conclusions, number 1, 2, and 3 in particular, we see that certain conclusions are being made about how the Croats in Central Bosnia are threatened, the supremacy of the Muslim units, and proposals for asking -- for assistance from the Republic of Croatia. Can you please tell us a little bit about these events and the conclusions that were reached as a result of the events that were ongoing in Central Bosnia? And I mentioned this because there is this particular issue in this case that the Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in particular Herceg-Bosna, were ethnically cleansing themselves. They wanted to ethnically cleanse their compatriots from Central Bosnia in order to create a more homogenous Croatian area in Herzegovina. Could you -- so in light of that, could you please comment on that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that session of the HVO of the HZ HB, they discussed the situation on the ground as it existed and among its features were problems with mobilisation and the complications created by large number of refugees in that area. Secondly, the session was held immediately after the Croats or the HVO had lost Travnik. Thirdly, it was held in the context of the definite failure of Vance-Owen Plan on the ground. So that was the context of this session. Many proposals were put forward, some were more radical, some were less radical, but it is obvious that the HVO was taken by surprise by the situation, it wasn't prepared for it, especially when it comes to the areas inhabited by Croatian people where there were units of the HVO outside of HZ HB, for example, Tuzla. There was a brigade of the HVO there and then there were places like Bihac, Sarajevo, and a number of other places outside of the territory of HZ HB. So this session and some other similar sessions held at the time show in a very clear way that there was no plan to move these people, these units, from those areas to some imagined, compact territory that the Croats considered as their own. Simply speaking, had there been such a plan, the consequences both for Croatian people as a whole and for these circumstances would have been completely different. For those reasons, they attempted to take appropriate measures ad hoc, they proposed them, with the intention to provide some sort of assistance to the people residing in the territories outside of the reach of the HZ HB authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01275, these are minutes from 18 June 1993, only a few days later. And of course if we look at the agenda, we can see from items 7 to 17 that in spite of all that was happening tabled are approximately ten draft decrees for discussion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at -- I won't ask you to discuss item 1, but this may be something that the Trial Chamber may wish to go in depth. But there is a reference to a military council being constituted, and then of course we can see that under item 2 on page 3 it says: "In keeping with the decree of the armed forces of the HZ HB form a military council which would contribute to the assessment of the military and political situation ..." If you could please tell us whether -- what was that counsel supposed to do exactly and whether in fact it was constituted. This would be page 2 for you.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 18 of the decree on the armed forces envisages the establishment of a military council. Article 18 says that a military council should be set up within the defence department, that it should deal with developing the armed forces and providing equipment for the armed forces. The council should comprise the president of the defence department, the chief of the Main Staff of the HVO of the HZ HB, as well as a certain number of members nominated by the president of the HZ HB. These are the powers of the military council and this is its composition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, there are some other matters being discussed here with respect to Mostar municipality. For the Trial Chamber's information, I won't be discussing this. We will be having Mr. Zubak here as I understand it as a witness; however, if the Trial Chamber wishes to pose any questions with respect to that part of the minutes, then you can do that now, otherwise I'll move on to the next document. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, regarding this document I just have one question. This meeting of the 43rd Session of the Croatian Defence Council of Herceg-Bosna takes place on June the 18th, 1993, at 10.00 a.m., you attended that session as well as other personalities. And one of the agenda items is the issue of those different decrees, and I noted that there was a decree on the appointment of judges and prosecutors during that meeting. I have the feeling, but correct me if I'm wrong, I have a feeling that those decrees were prepared, submitted to general approval; and after everyone's approval the decrees, but only after that, the decrees can be published in the gazette. Since in Herceg-Bosna there was no parliament, legislative texts were adopted during that type of meeting. Am I right in describing the functioning of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, Your Honour. I spoke about that yesterday. Once the HVO has adopted a certain decree law and once this has been submitted to the Official Gazette of the HZ HB for publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Therefore, it means that all the texts that are adopted are approved collectively, and had anyone disagreed he would have said so and there would have been a debate on that particular text. So the -- it operated somehow like a legislative assembly, but since there was an emergency situation, a war situation, this is the way texts were being carried; is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In a peacetime situation this is something that would be prescribed by law, and this law would be passed by the parliament. This was, however, no peacetime situation and there was no parliament. As to how the HVO took its decisions, the procedure for the adoption of laws, or something that was prescribed in the book of rules of the HVO, where the decision-making process was laid out in detail for the HVO. I will try to sum this up. The rules and procedures says that decisions should be adopted by the HVO by a majority vote. As soon as there is a majority that exceeds 50 per cent and as soon as there is a quorum, the decision is considered as adopted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to talk about the role of Mr. Prlic in these sessions. If I got it right, all the decrees were developed by the departments in charge of those particular decrees, for example, the appointment of prosecutors and judges - this is something I mentioned earlier - were developed on the basis of justice department proposals. This is at page 6 of the document. So each department prepares its own texts which are put on the agenda. Now, as regards to preparatory work, did the president of the HVO, Mr. Prlic, give order or did he just wait for the meeting and let each relevant department do the preparatory work as necessary? And during the meeting, as we can see here during the 43rd Session, he could speak, if necessary, against the text, say, I do not agree with the text, there needs to be a vote, and this is it. So summarizing, would the work and act befall in the development phase of the decree, so before the meeting, or would he just take the floor during the meetings and approve or reject the text as everyone else? In other words, had each department completely waited draft a text which was fit for purpose, so to say, and trying to meet the needs that arose, as we could see earlier on with the employment contract? So this would have meant that there was a collective vote when adopting the text on the basis of texts drafted by departments which were fairly autonomous and independent from the president of the HVO? So what do you say to this? Because you attended such meetings and you were in the -- you were in a very good position to answer this question. Of course Mr. Prlic could as well, but he cannot testify so he cannot share his point of view with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said yesterday, at the time in the HZ HB there was a single filter, unfortunately, before legal document came to a session of the HVO. This was the commission for regulations that I was in charge of and our remit was limited. We could propose amendments to a draft or perhaps some corrections. Once a draft of such a normative text or a decree was presented at a meeting and when this item of the agenda came up, Mr. Prlic would open the discussion on that item and ask the contributor, the presenter, if you like - and normally this was a head of department - to provide some sort of introduction and to present their reasoning. This opening or introduction would normally take between five and ten minutes, no longer than that, and then the president of the HVO would open the discussion on this proposal. And then everyone else was free to make suggestions or proposals in relation to the draft being tabled. There would often be the case if very few members decided to discuss a certain item of agenda, those heads of department who directly or indirectly were involved because the regulation pertained to the work of their departments; but sometimes Mr. Prlic would join in with his own suggestions, observations, and remarks. As soon as the debate was over, the president would conclude by making a proposal that could have gone two ways. One was to rework or refine the draft following this discussion, and once the draft was refined it would be forwarded to the HVO. If there were no serious objections about the draft, he would then order a vote and then a vote would be taken to see if a decree was adopted or not depending on the outcome of the vote. When it comes to this, I have to say that this wasn't necessarily taken by a show of hands. Sometimes it was obvious that there was a consensus and then the president would simply say, All right, debate over, regulation adopted. I would like to go through all the remaining ones now, and if he noticed that no one opposed this then he would say, Fine, I hereby conclude that such and such a decree or regulation is adopted and then we would move on to the next item on the agenda. If I may, just one thing that I believe to be important. The rules and procedures made it possible for any member of the HVO, if they could not agree, to file or submit a separate, dissenting opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like you -- I would like to thank you for this clarification. I thought this was the way things were going, but it's good to have this for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01669. It's 5 July 1993. We see your name there as being present, and just focusing your attention very briefly on item 2 it says here, under item 2 -- on paragraph that: "The municipal HVO shall harmonize its decisions and other documents in the procedure and conditions to allocate the use of flats within provisions of this decree within 15 days after it comes into effect." This is item 2 concerning the draft decree on abandoned flats which was submitted by the commission for regulations of the HVO HZ HB. Could you comment briefly on that, please, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, up until this point in time we hadn't had a single regulation in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna dealing with this. We had a variety of solutions and we dealt with this through municipal regulations, but there was too much varied or too much diversity, and we deemed it necessary to have a regulation at the level of the entire Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna that would be binding for this entire area which included all the municipalities that were part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, thereby we also envisaged that these municipalities should reach some sort of coordination, some level of coordination, between their laws and this overriding regulation. The main need to have a regulation like this was to find accommodation for people in abandoned houses and flats. In a way, this regulation defines what it is that we defined as an abandoned flat at the time and under the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any questions on that I'll go on to the next document, which is 1D 01617. This is 12 July 1993. Again, if we look at the agenda we see from items 2 to 7 -- 1D 01611, 1611. We look at items 2 to 7, we see that again there are several draft decrees that are up for discussion, again in keeping with your previous answers to the President's question if we look at, for instance, item 6, we see two individuals, Galic and Zubak, proposing amendments and thereafter we see that the draft was adopted unanimously. So this was what you were referring to earlier when you were answering the President's question; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. And item 9 - we're not going to discuss it, I just bring it to the Court's attention in case they have any questions about a group that has been assigned to mobilise -- to monitor the mobilisation. Mr. Zubak will be here, as I indicated, but if the Court has any questions fine, otherwise I'll go to the next document. The next document is 1D 01672, and here this is 22nd July 1993. These are minutes. It does not reflect whether you were there, but I want to focus your attention on agenda item number 3, report of the chief of the Main Staff of the military and security situation in the territory of HZ HB, and of course item 3 we see that the report contained information about the situation on the fronts, particularly Bugojno, Livno, and Zepce. And we understand that you are from Livno. Now, could you please tell us whether you recall being at that meeting; and if so, what do you recall about this particular item on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at this meeting. The meeting was held late in the evening in Siroki Brijeg. Speaking of item number 3, the military and security situation in the area of those municipalities, it was General Petkovic who spoke. Roughly speaking, the situation was quite gloomy because the plot kept on thickening in terms of the war going on. He wanted to see how the generals saw the situation in Livno, Bugojno, and Zepce, and then I think there was a question raised by the president of the Bugojno HVO about the situation in Bugojno and about the fact that the army outnumbered the HVO by a ratio of 11:1 or 10:1. The general tried to soothe him and tell him that all the material and technical equipment was being secured for the HVO in Bugojno and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down, slow down. I mean, this is very important. If you would slow down, you would assist everybody. The translators are labouring very hard to be as exact as possible. Continue.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The general spoke about the situation in Bugojno in a bid to strike a note of optimism in this generally gloomy situation. He informed us that the much-needed material and technology would be supplied. He said that the morale of the HVO was at the required level and there was no need to be pessimistic in relation to the HVO's preparedness in terms of its ability to defend the area in eventuality of clashes with the BH army. I'm certain that what General Petkovic told us at the time was information that he had and that he had received from the HVO commanders over in Bugojno. There is not the slightest doubt in my mind that he was out to mislead us in any way whatsoever. Nevertheless, several days later clashes erupted in Bugojno virtually a day or two after the HVO lost this area in its entirety. This just goes to show how information that was reaching us from further afield, even military intelligence, could be unreliable and how difficult it was at the time to have a realistic assessment of the situation in certain areas, including in this case Bugojno, unless you were yourself of course physically present in a given area. I will point this out again, I have no doubt that the general would have liked nothing better than to inform us truthfully about the situation as it was; but I know that he was receiving such information from Bugojno and that was that. Unfortunately, the information proved to be inaccurate, and under the circumstances it was very difficult to make the right calls virtually on a daily basis and to deal with all these delicate issues on such a tight schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I was waiting for Mr. Karnavas to finish this document to ask the following question, still under this document because on this document there is a fundamental issue on which we have to think, we have to determine the role -- the military role of Mr. Prlic. There is a document here saying that on July the 22nd, 1993, there was a meeting between 8.00 and 11.00 p.m., so a three-hour meeting, with three agenda item, the third agenda item being the military situation. We know on the basis of those grounds, though unfortunately there is not the attendance list, it's a pity but there is no attendance list, but we know because you told us that you attended, we at least know that Mr. Prlic attended and that General Petkovic also attended, plus the person who drafted the report. And if we take a close look at that document, we all know that there were the heads of the municipalities because the presidents of the municipalities attended the meeting. So the third agenda item deals with the military situation. You told us that General Petkovic gave an update on the military situation when you answered Mr. Karnavas's question. There was reliable information but there was this update, this presentation, by General Petkovic. Now, I'd like to know the following, after Mr. Petkovic made his presentation, did he receive instructions from Mr. Prlic and other members on how to conduct military operations on the basis of the situation report or were there no such orders to General Petkovic because there was in the remit of Mr. Mate Boban who was the head of the army? So can you answer that question. So General Petkovic attends that meeting. Does he do so only to present a report and not to receive instructions or orders from the members of the meetings or is it the other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, at this meeting General Petkovic did no more than to inform those present about the overall military and security situation, primarily the military situation that prevailed in the area. Having presented this information, no discussion followed nor were any conclusions adopted or, indeed, guide-lines regarding this information. General Petkovic simply presented this information, he brought it to everyone's attention, and no further steps were taken at this meeting. This is exactly what the transcript shows us. Otherwise, it would have been the established practice if certain guide-lines were being adopted or conclusions to record those in the transcript, but this was nothing but information being presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question may be difficult because I personally would be unable to remember a meeting which took place over 15 years ago, but perhaps you have a better memory than mine. So in your recordation, does the defence minister, Mr. Stojic, did he attend or did he just say nothing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember if Mr. Stojic was there. I do, however, remember the meeting, the reason being this was the last meeting before the fall of Bugojno. It was based on what transpired at this meeting that I arrived at a conclusion. All the information we were receiving through all sorts of different channels was to be taken with a grain of salt. Another reason I remember this meeting is this, one of the things discussed at the meeting was the military and security situation in Livno and that was where my family lived. It is only natural in a situation like that, that one should focus even more on this as opposed to perhaps discussion of another area, simply because all of my nearest and dearest were still in the area, my parents, my relative, my friends, and so on and so forth. This is yet another reason why the meeting is so wedged in my memory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, following the President's question, you said that you did not remember whether Mr. Stojic attended this meeting, but in the minutes of this meeting of July 22nd, 1993, it says in discussion of item 1 that the head of the military department, Mr. Stojic, informed -- the head of the defence department, Mr. Stojic, informed the meeting on the implementation of the decision on mobilisation, so I believe he was probably there. What do you think of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to answer your question based on my recollections. There were over 30 people in that meeting. Based on my recollections, I couldn't say whether Mr. Stojic was there or not. If it says in the minutes that Mr. Stojic reported on some previous item, then I have no reason to doubt that Mr. Stojic was indeed there, although I personally do not remember that. I don't remember all of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. To finish off, regarding the military situation, as far as you remember Mr. Stojic did not take the floor after General Petkovic made his presentation; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have said that I don't remember that there was any discussion after the briefing by General Petkovic. I don't remember anybody discussing anything, including Mr. Stojic; and as I've said just now, I don't remember that Mr. Stojic was in the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'm looking at the clock, it's 10.30, I believe it's a time for a break, our only break this morning. This will be a 20-minute break and we will resume after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is now in session. Mr. Karnavas, you've used up three hours already.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm fully aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you have two hours left. Go ahead. The Judges did speak a lot and did take up a lot of your time. We know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I think that is important for the Judges to ask questions with these sorts of witnesses, and I would invite their full engagement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, picking up from the President's question, I want to ask you to be a little more concrete because as I understood the question in a more general sense was whether Dr. Prlic gave operational instructions or orders to the military. That's how I understood it. Now, we've seen the law, so de jure the Trial Chamber will be able to make an assessment and can ask you for further clarifications if need be. By de facto, if you can tell us in light of your engagement of your various positions with the HZ HB and the HR HB, and given that you've told us that you attended dozens and dozens of meetings, I think somewhere in the neighbourhood of 40 to 50 meetings, can you recall any instance where Dr. Prlic issued operational orders to the Main Staff or to anybody in the military for that matter?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, when I spoke of this document I said that the entire discussion under item 3 was concluded with a briefing of General Petkovic concerning the situation on the ground. Secondly, on the sessions which I attended, and those were mostly the sessions of the HVO of the HZ HB, I'm not aware of any situations nor did I witness any situations where such operative orders were issued by the president of the HVO, and this is something that is well illustrated by the minutes from all sessions. As for other meetings, I did not attend them so I cannot provide a direct answer to this question, whether there had been such meetings and whether there had been such situations. I do not remember any situations in the meetings that I attended where the president of the HVO issued any operative orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Well let me just follow-up one other on that. Recognising that you were not at any meetings, did you ever hear of any meetings taking place where Dr. Prlic would have issued or is reported to have issued such orders, recognising that this is hearsay but nonetheless this may be something for the Trial Chamber to consider.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go on to the next document, 1D 01813, this is the last document, again very brief answers if possible. We see that this is dated 18 September 1993. It's addressed to the supreme commander of the armed forces and to the president of the chamber of deputies of the HR HB, so now we're in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. If we look at the second page, at the end of the page, we see it's Dr. Jadranko Prlic, president of the government of the HR HB. And if we just glean through this document we see that it's about all forms of unlawfulness, there's a mention of a coordinating body having been established. The very last paragraph talks about a conclusion, that it was concluded to propose to the supreme commander of the armed forces of the HR HB that a meeting concerning these issues be held with the Main Staff and asking for clear positions. Now, two questions. One, were you aware of the activities that are being discussed in this particular document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that there were a number of actions including these that were aimed at preventing any unlawfulness and dealing with the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I have no further questions on this document. If the Trial Chamber has any questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a technical question. This document sent by Mr. Prlic to the supreme commander of the army, I guess it's Mr. Boban. I see it's also sent to the president of the chamber deputies of the HR HB. Why is it sent to this person, this president of the chamber of deputies? You told us that there were no meeting of members of parliament or deputies, so what does this mean exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a new situation. I spoke of the time when the HZ HB existed, when there was no parliament and there were no parliamentary sessions. Now this other period is the period when the Croatian republic of HB was already established with all of its institutions, one of which was a legislative body, it was called the house of representatives. So this letter was sent to the president of this legislative body, I assume with the intention to have -- give -- have him say whether this body could act upon this and perhaps enact certain conclusions. So this is quite a new situation which emerged after the Croatian Republic of HB was established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to go on to another chapter and this deals with the Law on State Administration. There are just two documents on this. The first document is 1D 00822, and if we look at it and at the very top I believe we see the date of 20th of March, 1990. Now, this Law on State Administration, are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, this was the law that was being applied in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina having -- taking an -- having taken over this particular law from before, is that correct, or am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, if I may say so, the original law of the Croatian Republic of HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And is it -- according to the translation it says "the Croatian Republic of HB." Are we talking about the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or -- if you look at line 6 of your answer, page 38, you say: "This is ... the original law of the Croatian Republic of HB." Obviously you misspoke. What does this law purport to be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. Sometimes we need to make sure that the record is clear. All right. And was this Law on State Administration used by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a bit ago when we discussed the decree on taking over this law and applying it in the territory of HZ HB, we especially focused on the issue of relations between the municipal and republic inspection organs, so that was the decree that was taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And for the Trial Chamber they may be interested in looking at Articles 4, 7, and 8, as well as Article 62 for purposes of any questions; otherwise, I will move on to the next document and that would be 1D 00825. And we see that this is a decree on the proclamation on the Law on Amendments to the Law on State Administration. This is dated 26th March 1991 signed by President Alija Izetbegovic. And if we look at the law below it, look at Article 170 in particular, it says: "An official heading an administrative organ and his deputy may be relieved of their duties before the expiry of their term to which they were appointed if there is -- if this is required because of proportional representation of nations and nationalities of BH in the state administration and the implementation of personnel policies." And my first question is: On its face do you have an opinion as to whether this article, Article 170a, is constitutional?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, if I compare this article with the provisions with the Constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, I personally think it is unconstitutional.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now before we looked at this law, this labour law or that one segment that was passed at the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna where it talked about fixed terms, if you recall, and you gave us the reasoning for that, in particular because of the wartime situation; focusing on Article 170a, given that we have none other than Alija Izetbegovic promoting this concept, can you tell us whether in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, whether this article was ever applied. In other words, whether a particular individual because of his nationality was dismissed for reasons of proportional representation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm aware, not in the territory of HZ HB. I don't know of a single case where this article was applied and somebody was dismissed because of their ethnic origin in order for their position to be filled by a person of another ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I, Mr. Karnavas, would like to ask two questions. The first question is that you have said that in your view this article was unconstitutional. Could you tell more precisely, say more precisely, against what article or principle of the constitution it went. What's the violation? What's unconstitutional about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is contrary to the basic principle of equality of citizens before the constitution and the law. If you dismiss somebody because of their ethnic origin in order for a person of a different ethnic origin to be appointed to that same position, then in my view that represents the violation of the basic constitutional principle on equality of all citizens before the constitution and the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question is the difference -- what is the difference between nations and nationalities here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the legal system of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia under the term "nationality," or rather, the term "nationality" referred to national minorities; that is to say, in the former Yugoslavia the term "nationality" was used in the place of the term "nationality minority," that is to say Hungarians were a nationality, Romanians, Austrians, were all a nationality in the former SFRY. As for nations, those were the six constituent nations in the SFRY, Croats, Serbs, Montenegrins, Slovenes, Macedonians, and Bosnians, all of them had a status of constitutive nation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to go on to another topic and this deals with the rules of procedure, and we're going to focus on P 00596. And I should say this is how the document was introduced. The first page is -- in this document is irrelevant. It is the second page where we will find the rules of procedure of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna dated 17 October 1992, and that is the document that I wish to focus on. Do you recognise these Rules of Procedure, sir?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, we don't have much time, as much as I would love to have a discussion on this, we don't have much time. But I asked you a series of questions yesterday and perhaps we can focus just ever so briefly on Articles 40 and 41 and -- because they are somewhat interesting. Article 40 says: "If the Presidency of the HZ HB decides that a regulation or other piece of legislation of the HVO HZ HB is contrary to regulations or other acts by the Presidency of the HZ HB, it shall demand that the HVO readjust the regulation or other general acts or to take other appropriate measures within a given time-limit ..." And then I won't bother to read the second paragraph. Now, again based on your testimony, the Presidency is made up of the presidents of the municipalities; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, can we conclude that based on this what is being said that if these presidents of the municipalities don't like a -- or don't agree with the particular piece of legislation that has been introduced by the HVO HZ HB, they can demand that it be readjusted? Is that how it should be read?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I can give just two sentences. The rules of procedure envision a situation in which the Presidency of the HZ HB would continue adopting decree laws, and then it goes on to say that all enactments of other organs, including the HVO, under the principle of subordination have to be in compliance with all the decrees adopted by the Presidency. Then it goes on to say that should that not happen, then the Presidency may set aside such an enactment. In addition to others, the Presidency comprised the heads of the HVO municipalities because they as part of the Presidency were meant to adopt decree laws.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And based on that, if the president of a municipality didn't particularly care for a piece of legislation coming from the HVO, that president of the municipality, being also a member of the Presidency, would he or she have any influence and pass -- in having the Presidency demand the readjustment of the regulation to suit the particular HVO municipality or president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, there is a conflict of interest there because the president of the HVO in a municipality, as a member of the Presidency together with others, could in practice, block a legislation of the HZ HB if he believed that such a piece of legislation could harm or went against the interests of the municipal HVOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We'll go on to the next document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Additional question. Mr. Perkovic, are you aware of this rule, this article, ever being applied in practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, because approximately during this period of time, 1992, the Presidency of the HZ HB practically stopped meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. That corresponds to what I expected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, P 09530, and this is dated 12 November 1992. These are the Rules of Procedure of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We've seen this document before. I just want to touch on a couple of points very quickly in light of your testimony that we see on Article 9, for instance, it talks about: "The bodies of the HVO shall be bound to implement the programme of work and monitor its execution..." So we looked, I believe, at one particular programme of work unless I'm mistaken. This is what was being referred to; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This refers to programs of departments and commissions and implementation of tasks as provided by those programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And if we look at Article 13, for instance, it talks about: "Documents shall be submitted to the Office of the Secretary of the HVO with all necessary accompanying documents, including: The opinion of the "Commission for Regulation on Conformity of the Preliminary Draft," and so on and so forth. That's what you were talking about, you issuing opinions; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I believe you also testified that not always the proper procedure was being followed which made your job somewhat more difficult because then you would have to intervene during the sessions, that is?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here in the Rules of Procedure there is such a possibility, namely, that head of a department could insist that a certain item be placed on the agenda and naturally there were cases where precisely that happened, that they insisted on putting a certain regulation on the agenda even before that regulation had passed through the procedure as mandated by Article 13. So what I'm saying now is Article 18, last paragraph, namely, the person proposing some material can insist that this material be included on the agenda for a session, and this is something that the HVO would decide upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to ask a linguistic question. If you look at the English version in Article 13 you have "documents" and "documentation." However, if you look at the original, if I'm not mistaken, the first quote "documents" is here is called "materijali," and you yourself have now spoken of materials. Could you be so kind as to define what specifically is meant by the term "materials."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the legal slang the term "material" in BH refers to all documents provided together with the basic texts, so that would include the basic texts, the opinion of the legislative commission, perhaps even department for finance, and so on. So all of these texts put together would comprise material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That would then mean that the reference to accompanying documents is redundant because that's contained in materials; and furthermore, do I understand you correctly, I get the feeling that the basic text, as you say, is a draft legislation or another draft normative act?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basic text is a proposal for a regulation. So it would arrive to the session of the HVO in the form of a proposal, accompanied by opinions of relevant institutions. In the legal slang we use the term "material," but that's not a legal term, it's an informally used term, and I used it in the same manner here because it was a customary term.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In light of this question -- and of course I touched upon it yesterday a little bit, you told us that at the state level there were six or seven different filter stages where a draft would be looked at in order for it to be harmonized and ultimately passed. Now, having looked at the various legal instruments in preparation for your testimony and your previous testimony, do you see linguistic inconsistencies or redundancies? I mean, as a draftsman, do you see any errors that perhaps shouldn't be there or is every word that's contained in these documents as a result of a great deal of reflection and deliberation?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, Article 13 of the rules illustrates in the best possible way what I said yesterday, it confirms it. Three organs are mentioned here, out of which only one is duty-bound to provide opinion on each normative act and that is the Commission for Regulations. And this is why I spoke of just one filter. When it comes to the department of finance, they were duty-bound to give their opinion if that normative act entailed some expenditure of funds, of financial means. And the justice department would do the same if it involved some of their topics. Based on that, it was normal that due to this reduced procedure it was possible for certain inadequate terms to be included in proposals for regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to ask you to be a little bit more direct and concrete because of my time limitations because that answer at the very end could have been given to me at the forefront. Recognising that all of this is important, I would kindly ask you to be a little more concrete.
