Now, if we look at Article 34 and 35 in this very briefly, here Article 34 talks about: "A decree and decisions shall be published in the Narodni List ..." and then Article 35 talks about transparency. Now, there was an analyst expert from the OTP who did an assessment, he's supposedly an constitutional expert, he sits on the Slovenian constitutional court, and he had some opinions regarding the usage of the Narodni List, the Official Gazette. And as I recall, his opinion was that the use of this was also another indication of taking on state-like powers and institutions because only at the state level would you have an Official Gazette. Now, could you clarify that for us. Was that correct? Prior to the war was only the state, and that would be -- or the republic, for instance, publishing Official Gazettes or did municipalities also have Official Gazettes? That's the first question.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the war, just like nowadays, all municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina have their Official Gazettes where they publish their normative acts. It goes for municipality, for states, and nowadays even cantons and entities in BH. That is to say, our legal tradition is that all levels of authorities had their official publications where they published their enactments and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And just to make sure that we're absolutely clear, this expert was from Slovenia, Ljubljana, a little further away from Zagreb. Now, he's a constitutional professor on the constitutional court, his father was a big man in the Tito era. Is it possible that somebody with his qualifications would not know the answer that you just gave us or is it in Slovenia, for instance, you know, during that period and thereafter they had a different legal tradition; hence, why as an expert he was trying to convince the Judges that this sort of publishing of an Official Gazette would be the same -- would be indicative of state-like powers?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it's possible that this person didn't know this. Slovenia had, and I believe still has, almost the same legal tradition as Bosnia-Herzegovina. Also, in Slovenia all the municipalities up until its proclamation of independence had their Official Gazettes, local ones, municipal ones, I believe they still do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go through now the next series of documents very quickly because we talked about these Rules of Procedure. If we -- just to verify, 1D 02518, here we have the Rules of Procedure for the Siroki Brijeg municipality. Have you had a chance to look at these rules; and if so, are they consistent with what was in practice at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a chance to look at these. This is mostly in keeping with the usual, established practice and procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And in particular what I'm most interested in, because we're going to talk -- I'm going to go through all these documents very quickly. With respect to the collective organ aspect of it, because I did ask you whether this was something that had been in place prior to the elections and thereafter. So do -- do these Rules of Procedure also reflect that the Croatian Defence Council of the Siroki Brijeg municipality is acting as a collective organ?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Let me bring to your attention Article 4, paragraph 2, saying that the HVO takes its decisions at sessions convened by a majority vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, just very quickly because the Court can look at these later, 1D 01118. These are the Rules of Procedure for Capljina. Are these more or less representative and consistent with the rules that we find for Siroki Brijeg? And again, speaking of the collective body aspect of it.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a similar document, quite similar in fact, and it's based on exactly the same principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what about 1D 02052? This is for the municipality of Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at 1D 00869 here dated 5 December 1992, this is for the Tuzla municipality. If we look at Article 2 it talks about: "The Presidency shall work and reach decisions in its session as a collective organ and shall be collectively responsible for its work. Would this also be similar?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. The principle is the same and the text is almost identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if we look at Article 6, keeping with our initial discussion we picked up from yesterday with respect to stamps or seals, we see that: "The Presidency shall have a round stamp ... in diameter, with the following elements: In the middle, the temporary coat of the arms of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina," and so on and so forth. So here we see, do we not, that Tuzla is also adopting a seal, and I don't see any reference to -- about a seal law to the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Article 6. I don't see any reference to that. So is Tuzla doing anything different, I guess that's the question of the day, is Tuzla doing anything different then that was done in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna with respect to having a seal?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not doing anything different as opposed to the organs in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The Law on Seals of Bosnia-Herzegovina says that these seals must have the coat of arms of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this law was never changed or amended. We see Tuzla placing in their seal a temporary, provisional, coat of arms of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They are adapting their own internal laws to the needs of the situation as it developed on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we look at the next document, 1D 02012, this is for the municipality of Soli and again having had a chance to look at it would this more or less reflect what you've indicated before about this being a collective body, that is, the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Soli?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but with the following proviso. This is not the municipality of Soli, this is the Croatian Community of Soli and it didn't have any attributes of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that clarification. And finally, 1D 01879, here we have the Rules of Procedure of the Chamber of Deputies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. Are you familiar with these rules; and if so, how and what do they purport to be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. Essentially, this book of rules envisages rules for the functioning of the Chamber of Deputies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, it also envisages their rights and duties, the way in which they should work, and it also provides for any other issues that are important for the work of the Chamber of Deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Unless there are any questions, I will go on to the next brief topic which deals with defence plans, it's something that has come up in this courtroom. If we look at document 1D 00897, we don't have the entire English version of it because it's a rather lengthy law but it's the law on All People's Defence. And we see it's dated 9 February 1984. I believe you did tell us that you served -- you did your military service and you have commented about having to also report in your hometown when you returned to Livno back in 1992, I believe. So are you familiar with the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would be shocked if you weren't, actually. If we look at page 3, Article 46, the rights and duties of local communities. Just very briefly for the record we see seven items: "Organized and prepared -- organize and -- for armed fight, organize and prepare the civil protection, draft and adopt defence plan, organize and execute training, organize and implement the preparation for mobilisation, organize craft production and homemade production, determine the organization of the organs of the local community and preparing them in the training of the executing of the war tasks." Do you know whether this Law on All People's Defence continued to apply after the elections and after Bosnia-Herzegovina declared itself to be independent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And of course we're going to be discussing or seeing an example of number 3: "Draft and adopt defence plan and plans for other emergency situation of the local community." Are you familiar with what is being discussed here about the drafting of a defence plan? What is a defence plan for those of us who did not grow up in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Defence plans are based on the fundamental -- the notion for defence in the former Yugoslavia. The assumption was that people would be armed and would put up resistance, and each individual would be committed to the defence of the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would have the duty to defend the country. This applied equally to military conscripts and to all other adult citizens of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. Within that same framework, all levels of government throughout Yugoslavia had to have defence plans that would apply in the eventuality of an aggression. In addition to the official authorities, this obligation applied to any other legal entities, such as companies, schools, universities, theatres, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you. It's one of my favourite topics but we don't have much time to dwell on it in fact. If we look at 1D 02722, now we're going to look at a series of four documents just to show how it works a little bit. Here we see -- this is a procedure upon receiving the Leotar signal. Have you had a chance to look at this document and could you tell us whether this is the sort of procedure that you would expect emanating from the application of the Law on All People's Defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've had a chance to look at the document, yes. This document, the procedure for the reception of signals, this is something that was applied in Capljina municipality, but this had to remain in keeping with the Law on All People's Defence. For something like this to take effect, certain procedures had to be followed and certain approvals obtained.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 1D 02723, this is an extract from the plan of relocation municipal administrative organs to wartime locations, and we see that the municipal administrative organs and state organs is the Karaotok hotel with its auxiliary facilities. Now, do you see this and can you please explain to us what exactly is this all about? And you have to look at the next page, of course, which is the decision to designate wartime locations, I ask this because in particular because we do know about the siege of Sarajevo. We've heard testimony that there were some in the Presidency that argued that the War Presidency should function outside of Sarajevo for better or for ill, but could you please explain this document. This might be able to assist us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We talked about these defence plans. According to these defence plans, each municipality and each socio-political organization had reserve positions in terms of location, and if there was an imminent threat of war or if there were war it was to move to that reserve location so that it could continue its work. And the same thing applied to the republican organs of administration over in Sarajevo, including the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. According to the republic's defence plan, there is a location or the reserve position that it would withdraw to was Han Pijesak, which is a small town 40 kilometres north of Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. All right. And that's underground as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's an underground military base.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Of course that would not have been available during that period because of the Republika Srpska; correct? And as I understand it, those facilities might even have been used by Mr. Mladic himself, General Mladic, afterwards.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at 1D 02724, okay, this is in keeping with the previous document. Now here we have a decision to approve the defence plan of the Capljina municipality. So it would appear when we look at this that actually one not only has to come up with a defence plan but it actually has to be approved; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said a while ago. There had to be an appropriate procedure first for adoption and approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, you did indicate that enterprises as well as schools and other facilities had to have their own defence plan, and by way of an example let's look at 1D 02811 and this is a decision that -- if we were to look in the third page, we see it's January 13, 1989, it's a decision on adopting the defence plan for the printing company Graficar in Doboj, which today would be the Republika Srpska. And so -- and this is a 200 -- the plan, the actual plan in the original language is approximately 200 pages. If you could just briefly tell us, would this represent what a typical defence plan would look like? And again, if we see on number 1, there's the plan of readiness, mobilisation plan, operational plan, utilisation plan for territorial defence, utilisation plan for civil protection, plan for security and self-protection measures, communications, and crypto-protection plan. Is this something that we would -- is this the typical defence plan that would have been prepared and available by the enterprises and others as a result of the All People's Defence that was in effect even after Bosnia-Herzegovina declared itself independent?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a complete defence plan for a company. The law precisely defines what elements any and each plan should comprise. This depended on the legal entity in question. We have a complete defence plan here for a company containing all the subplans, saying exactly what the company should do in the eventuality of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the defence plan for this company is quite interesting. It's several pages long but it dates back to the 1980s. I assume that you were not able to find any other defence plan, but I assume that the companies existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and especially in Herzegovina had their own defence plan. This is just an example, right, it is not in the period of reference. But I believe that you meant that all companies had their own defence plan. That was your point, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's correct, and as I understand these plans are normally confidential. This was outdated and hence we were able to get our hands on it, but the witness can certainly verify it and I did have one other follow-up question which was:

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These plans based on the All People's Defence, are they considered operational plans for military purposes or are they plans for civil protection reasons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the plans actually included both these components. These plans were a complete answer to the activities of the legal entity, a company in this case, during an imminent threat of war or a state of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Unless there are any other questions, I will continue on with my next topic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one additional question briefly. Today in the Federation, could you tell us whether companies still have this kind of defence plan or is another defence concept in force now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. President, the situation has changed and has changed radically. We were looking at the situation when the only thing around were state-owned companies. These days you have thousands of small private companies, private enterprises. The place is teeming with those. Sometimes they only have one or two employees and they're under no obligation to do this. Now, there is a new programme for defence in Bosnia and Herzegovina. That is the order of the day in keeping with more Western rules and standards, there is now a professional army and this whole concept has been left behind arming the people who then go up and put up resistance, and that was the very foundation of what we have been talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just to touch-up on that last answer, the JNA certainly was a professional army; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA, it comprised two components, the professional component and military conscripts in the sense of persons performing their regular and compulsory military term which was normally one year. There was the professional component and the non-professional component.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But also in keeping with the military doctrine, as I understand it, in the former Yugoslavia you had the JNA but you also had the Territorial Defences at the local level and they were to work in conjunction; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The concept of defence implied some form of coordinated activity between the JNA and the Territorial Defence, but the JNA was a federal institution and the state was in charge of the JNA. As far as the Territorial Defence was concerned, this was something that each of the republics was in charge of. Bearing that assumption in mind, when the war broke out these two components of the JNA started clashing on the one hand and the units of the Territorial Defence on the other because essentially units of the Croatian Defence Council and the brigade of the Croatian Defence Council in the municipalities rested on this principle of Territorial Defence. That was the principle and that was the concept and that's what they were based on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to switch on to another topic dealing with municipalities --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Karnavas, because with your question you drew my attention to another point. You said that when the JNA existed there was coordination between JNA and Territorial Defence. That's fine. But while you were saying this I wondered whether between the HVO, the military units of the HVO and the municipalities, maybe as Territorial Defence, there existed anything. So to your knowledge, could there be a coordination or not or maybe you just cannot answer this question. Maybe this is not relevant to your knowledge. But there used to be coordination between the JNA and Territorial Defence earlier. So to your knowledge, I would like to know whether between the military units of the HVO, brigades, and so on and the municipalities whether there was coordination, military coordination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You see, I was talking about legal solutions, and what this implied was the coordination of all of the JNA's activities with the Territorial Defence forces of each of the republics. One thing I can say as any other citizen who lived in the area is that as the crisis in the former Yugoslavia first started emerging, the concept kept on working, quite successfully in fact. However, following the multi-party elections in most of the republics, the two principles of defence and the two organizations started clashing. What happened? The JNA tried, and succeeded in some places, in entirely disarming the Territorial Defence units to varying degrees of success depending on the place of course. At a later stage this escalated and became an all-out conflict in Slovenia and later in Bosnia and Herzegovina between the JNA units on the one hand and the Territorial Defence units on the other, and this wasn't just about the HZ HB but virtually in all the areas affected by the conflict, predominantly Croat and predominantly Bosniak areas, such as the one in Tuzla, for example, clashes between the JNA units and the Territorial Defence units there, in Sarajevo, in Herceg-Bosna, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not really answer my question. This is what I wanted to know. I would like to know whether at the level of the HVO -- I'm not talking about the JNA here. I'm talking about the relations between HVO and municipalities. Let me be very specific. General Petkovic, for example, or General Praljak, could any of these gentlemen coordinate what they were doing with the president of municipalities, for example, Mr. Kordic or Mr. Topic from Mostar regarding military activities, or in the framework of what existed at the time is it the HVO as the military component which controlled everything as far as the military was concerned and the municipalities in this case would only be contributing to logistics by paying, for example, for the soldiers or by billeting them but did not have a say when it comes to coordination or military activities. I'd like to know what the relation was between the military component of the HVO and the municipalities. To sum things up, I would like to know whether someone like Kordic had any importance as far as military matters were concerned or Mr. Topic from Mostar or was it the military component of the HVO that totally controlled everything? Maybe you can't answer, say so if you can't; and if you have the answer, please give it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for clarifying the question. According to the decree on the armed forces of the HZ HB all the municipal brigades of the HVO were subordinated to the HVO's Main Staff, I'm talking about the HVO of the HZ HB. In that sense, there was subordination, subordination of the Main Staff of the HVO of the HZ HB --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat the last part of the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did that always apply 100 per cent when the realities on the ground were concerned, I don't really know, but I can't rule out the possibility of certain municipal leaders of the HVO influencing the situation in a brigade and overall perhaps behaviour of certain units of the HVO. But according to the regulations of Herceg-Bosna they were all subordinated to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now we're going to go on to another topic which deals with municipalities, and that's -- fits into what we were just discussing. And there are a series of documents and I'm just going to cover some of them, not all of them, but the first batch of documents deal with Livno and that's a place that you're very familiar with. If we look at 1D 00796, for instance, here we see a decision by the Livno municipality to declare the state of emergency, correct, and it's Livno itself that's doing this? 1D 00796.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this document. It was adopted by the Municipal Assembly in Livno municipality. This was not an isolated case in Livno municipality. This was done by other municipalities as well at the time when the imminent threat of war was approaching those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And let's look at some other documents that might be relevant to that, 1D 00795, this document is a decision to appoint a Presidency of the Livno Municipal Assembly, and this is dated 4 April 1992. And as I understand your testimony, that's what you found when you returned to Livno, this War Presidency was in a sense active, is that correct, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The document is from May of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- not August, as you said, and when I came to Livno this Presidency had already been functioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then of course if we look at the names -- the Trial Chamber can look at those names they will be able to see who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, exactly. I've just seen a name and in this document number 7, president of the Livno SDA, the SDA is Muslim, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they were Bosniaks, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So there was this municipal Presidency at the time and it was made up of Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and Serbs. The president of the Serbian Democratic Party was in the Presidency as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document, 1D 00802, this is a decision we see, again from Livno, and it talks about who will be considered refugees and also says: "Men liable for military service between the ages of 17 and 60 as well as women between the ages of 18 and 50 ... cannot have refugee status." So here again this is the municipality making this particular decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we look at 1D 00805, this is a mobilisation and demobilisation of assets. Again, this is -- this shows that it is the municipality that is taking matters unto its own, as it had the right to do so; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The next document is 1D 00808. This is a statutory decision to establish provisional municipal authorities during state of war or imminent threat of war, and if we look at, for instance, Article 5, this is "the Municipal Assembly of Livno shall retain the right to exercise political control over the work of the Livno OHVO, including the right to a vote of confidence ..." Can you explain that just very briefly, and this is dated 29 August 1992.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very interesting statutory decision, it's interesting because it maintains the functioning of the Municipal Assembly and its active role because it establishes that the HVO is to report on its work to the Municipal Assembly once a month. This is an interesting decision because it represents a very significant difference in relation to the decision on establishing HR HB, which says that the HVO is appointed by the municipal HVOs. Therefore, when one analyses this decision it can be easily concluded that they simply reshaped the executive organ and its name into the Executive Board of the HVO, whereas it maintained the same responsibility and same subordination in relation to the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. You talked about a decision. In the record it says "HR HB" and what I believe what you meant was HZ HB, is that correct, not HR. You say -- you talk about a decision on establishing the HR HB, which says that the HVO is appointed by the municipal HVOs." Are we talking about the HR or are we talking about the HZ, the Croatian Community or the Croatian Republic?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the date, it is clear that this refers to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I was referring to the decree of HVO of HZ HB, where it says that the HVO of the HZ HB is -- or rather, appoints the municipal HVOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'm not sure I fully comprehend your answer. Let's take it one step -- a little slower on this. This is -- if we look at -- this is a statutory decision to establish provisional municipal authorities during the state of war. And Article 2 talks about: "A municipal Croatian Defence Council of Livno is hereby established ... as the highest authority within the framework of the rights and obligations of the municipality. It shall assume all powers of the Municipal Assembly ... and the Executive Committee of the Municipal Assembly ..." Okay. So that's Article 2. Now, Article 5 says: "The Municipal Assembly of Livno shall retain the right to exercise political control over the work of the Livno municipal defence council, including the right to a vote of confidence in the Livno municipal defence council as a whole or as individual members ..." All right. Now, if you could once again tell us why is this significant because here it would appear that the Municipal Assembly is reserving the right on exercising political control in a vote of confidence, which means also I would suspect a vote to dismiss someone. So could you please explain that.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Article 5 actually says that the Municipal Assembly continues with its work even though that's somewhat contradictory in relation to Article 2, where it says that the HVO would take over all of its competencies. However, when it comes to the functioning of the authorities in the municipality, it is clear that the Municipal Assembly continued performing its function in a certain way, and the HVO was duty-bound to report to it on its work.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But these appointments, if I'm not mistaken, are they done by the HVO HZ HB, the executive authority, that is; or are they being done by the local municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the decree of the HVO of the HZ HB, they were to be appointed by HZ HB, and in the case of this municipality and some other municipalities it was done by Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So de facto at least we see how it's -- and de jure how the municipalities dealt with that issue, irrespective of the statutory decision, correct, the statutory decision establishing the HVO HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If we go on to the next document very quickly, this is 1D 00810. Here we have a decision on temporary sanction for evasion of military service. Again, this is being handled at the municipal level; correct? So, for instance, to put it in a more concrete fashion, had you -- when you showed up in Livno had you not registered, this decision would have kicked into place because you would have been avoiding your military service at least by not even showing up and registering to see what duties, if any, they were going to appoint you to. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, your comment is correct. Had I not volunteered to do that, somebody could have reported me of being there and then this decision on penalties would have applied to me for avoiding my military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Sticking with Livno, 1D 00811, this is a decision on the organization and range of responsibilities of the Livno responsibility -- Livno municipal Croatian Defence Council. Again, were you familiar with this particular decision and does this represent what was in place during the time as you -- we're talking about 21 September 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with this decision. It is essentially based on the decisions of the HZ HB regulating or setting forth the minimum number of departments and the structure of the municipal HVOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 1D 00812, this is a decision to prohibit the entry of refugees into Livno municipality, and again this is based on a decision taken up by the Livno municipality; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. However, they see -- they use an obviously wrong term here the whole time. This -- these are not refugees. These are the deported persons, persons who were from other municipalities of Bosnia and Herzegovina and wanted to come to the Livno municipality as refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: These were displaced persons?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. 1D 00 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I find here the term "prohibit entry to refugees in TO Livno municipality," TO means normally Territorial Defence, but what does this refer to here? Maybe it is a misprint?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please read the title in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Me? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please read it in Croatian, Mr. Perkovic, so we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Decision on Prohibiting the Entry of Refugees into the Territory of Livno Municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously this is a mistake in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And "territory" is "podrucju."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let's not go there, Your Honour. 1D 00317.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is a decision to appropriate property of the occupier and requisition of the property for the needs of the defence of the Livno municipality, so here again this is a municipal decision; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And lastly, again, just to finish off on Livno, 1D 01362, we see here that pursuant to Article 48 of the statute of the party of the democratic action at its meeting held on 27th May 1993, there's a decision passed, senior consultant Dr. Junuz Cero is hereby appointed to the commission for assessing war damage. Can you comment on this very briefly, what does this decision mean? This is signed by president of the Livno SDA.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may. We've seen several documents about Livno and it's all related to the period September/October 1992 and now we're in May 1993, and I wonder how Mr. Perkovic could talk about it when at that time he was not having any --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll lay a foundation, Your Honour. I guess the objection would be lack of foundation for this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you familiar with the situation in Livno at or about in May 1993; and if so, could you please tell us how? You did tell us earlier that you had your parents, your close ones -- your near ones and dear ones, I believe that's how it was translated, but could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every weekend when I was free I would travel to Livno. In addition to my family home in Livno, I had no other apartment or house. During the working week in Herzegovina when I was there, I lived in a hotel and I would spend all my weekends in Livno.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Are you familiar with the Livno Municipal Board as it's reflected above here, it's the -- I mean, from looking at this it would appear that the gentleman, the president of the Livno SDA, is part of the Livno municipal government. If I'm mistaken, please correct me; if I'm not, then I guess we can just move on. I think the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In May of 1993 representatives of the SDA and HDZ worked together within the municipal authorities in Livno. This is just another confirmation of the fact that they were in power together because one member of the SDA was appointed to one of the municipal commissions, in this particular case commission for assessing war damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, due to time constraints, I'm just going to read the documents, they are in order, I'm just going to ask you more or less one global question and if the Trial Chamber has any other questions they could certainly ask you. But with respect to the next document, 1D 02058, this is on Siroki Brijeg. Have you looked at this document and are you familiar with it? Just a yes or no would do and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look on to the next document, 1D 01115, this is a decision to organize all the responsible for the functioning of the living and working capacities. This is Capljina/Stolac -- Capljina, I believe, the Capljina municipality. Have you looked at this document? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we look at 1D 01212, again this is a decision on establishing all functions related to life and work and this is Stolac; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we move on to Tuzla we see 1D 01369, this is a decision establishing the Presidency of the Municipal Assembly. This is 3 April 1992. Have you looked at this document?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Next document, again dealing with Tuzla, 1D 01157, this is an order on the eviction of the illegal tenants of socially owned flats in Tuzla municipality, of course it refers to a Crisis Staff order. Have you looked at this decision and are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Next document, 1D 01172, this is an order and it should say on the work obligation to execute a decision on work duty. We see it's the Crisis Staff with the municipality of Tuzla dated 25 May 1992, I take it you have looked at this document as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We look at 1D 01170, consistent with other documents that we have seen here, there's an order to mobilise conscripts of Tuzla municipality. You have looked at this as well; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then 1D 01385, this is an order evicting persons and property from unlawfully occupied socially owned flats, and we see under Article 1 it says to be -- an order to immediately vacate, and there's -- there's no right of appeal. This is 1D 01385, Tuzla; correct? You looked at this before, have you not?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then if we look at 1D 01392, this is an order on the obligation of carrying out the decision on work obligation, and of course this is Tuzla, and if you were to focus on Article II, Roman numeral II, any abuse and failure to follow this order or delay of its implementation shall be most severely punished, and of course the most severe punishment at that point in time was the death penalty, correct? Not that it was ever applied but that's what was the most severe punishment; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: It would be helpful if you could enlighten the Chamber on the relevance of all these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The relevance of these documents, Your Honour, and there are hundreds more, but I'm just giving you what I would say a vignette, is to show how the municipalities were operating on their own and how they were doing things on their own instituting various legislative acts, how they would handle a conscript issue, how they would deal with abandon property issues, and so on and so forth. It is relevant. Tuzla of course is used to show that there is no distinction when it comes to looking at and comparing the legislative acts and conduct, it would appear that what is happening is Tuzla, although to my understanding nobody from the Tuzla municipality has been prosecuted in this Tribunal nor is being considered to be prosecuted for these sorts of acts. So we see that the same sort of activity is happening in Tuzla as is happening elsewhere. And it would appear, at least this is part of our theory of the Defence why it's relevant, that the municipalities are trying to respond to the exigent circumstances and to the situations that have been forced upon them because we have already seen testimony that Sarajevo is no longer -- is blocked, the state for all intents and purposes has failed and is failing to carry out its obligations. And so we talked about the All People's Defence, we've talked about the constitution allowing at the municipal level for people to self help and engage in certain activities, so all of this fits into our theory, and that is what is happening at the municipal level is rather consistent across the broad throughout the free territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and therefore we should not be singling out one group against another. So that's the overall framework. And also, if you look at the relationship between the executive authority, for instance, and at the municipal level, we do see at the municipal level a certain independence [realtime transcript read in error "dependence"] and so -- then we were pointed out to one instance where, at the municipal level, irrespective of what was at the statutory decision of the HVO HZ HB that the municipal -- the municipality is acting on its own. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm very grateful to you, Mr. Karnavas. I think you've succeeded in showing --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe on line 9 it should be independence, "certain independence" as opposed to "dependence." Independence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, we would like the witness to answer because all your explanation after my colleague's question could have been presented to us in the form of questions asked to the witness and we would like the witness to answer -- to state what you have just stated to the extent that he may agree or disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I just have one last document, Mr. President, and that would be 1D 00867. This is a decision to form a Presidency of the Tuzla municipality Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Those are the documents that I wanted you to look at -- you have looked at them, in fact, as I understand, and would you please tell us: Do these documents based on your activities, your involvement, your experience at the time and thereafter, do they reflect what was happening in the various municipalities? That's question number one. And question number two: When you compare these legal instruments from the various municipalities that were within, say, Herceg-Bosna and you compare them with Tuzla municipality, do we see any real difference or are these municipalities in essentially acting more or less consistently?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, I deeply regret that we don't have more time for me to give a detailed explanation. I will try to give an answer as explicit as possible. The documents that we are discussing now show very well that in that period of time practically all municipalities acted on their own initiative, adopting regulations which they believed to be the best ones, given the situation in each municipality and disregarding higher enactments, be those of Bosnia and Herzegovina or of HZ HB in relation to its administrative organs. In order to prove this, I will give you two examples, the ones that you quoted, document 1D 02058, the decision on temporary organization of executive power and municipal administration in the territory of Siroki Brijeg, that is to say in the territory of HZ HB. Let me just remind you, Article 5, penultimate paragraph says that president, vice-president, and members of the HVO are appointed and dismissed by the Municipal Assembly and that upon proposal of the president of the HVO, the Municipal Assembly may appoint and dismiss other members. This decision is dated 20th of November, 1992; that is to say, period of time when the Croatian Defence Council had been functioning for three to four months, when there had already been other decisions of the HVO. And it is clear that this decision represents a significant departure from those decisions. In the similar way, the municipal organs of Tuzla in their decisions take a significant departure from the decisions of organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We see some decisions from Tuzla illustrating this. I will only point out two as an example. Document 1D 01385, which is a decision on evicting persons who had moved into apartments unlawfully. Under Roman II in the last sentence it says that: "Those who are ordered to move out have no right to appeal, which is contrary to all existing regulations of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time." Second example, document 1D 01392, which is a decision on work duty. It says that those persons who fail to act in accordance with that order will be punished in the -- in strictest terms. I don't think that Mr. Beslagic, president of the Tuzla Presidency meant to execute these people, no. It just shows the lack of power of all municipal organs in various municipalities at the time. It shows that they had no contact, no lines of communication with Sarajevo. All those lines were severed and the municipal organs throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina took steps that they saw as best under their circumstances, disregarding existing regulation be it regulation of HZ HB or the republic organs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you're saying is extremely interesting and very comprehensive, but it's time to stop. We can probably pick up on the same topic after we resume. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I just -- okay. Very well. Very well. I just want to make sure -- I want to strike while everything is hot in everybody's mind, but we can do that when we get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's time for a break. We have no more tape. So we will resume at 2.15 p.m. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.37 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. Yes, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, just for the record I would like to raise an objection about the admission of the -- the way the last ten documents before the break were introduced by counsel for Mr. Prlic. In my opinion -- I just -- it can't be right that the witness is first being given no opportunity to discuss any of these ten documents but simply has to say, Yes, I saw the document in preparation for this testimony and that we don't have a long speech from Mr. Karnavas explaining the relevance of all this evidence. And then subsequently -- all is in front of the witness and then subsequently the witness again testifying about these documents this just can't be proper procedure, and we object.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may -- just very briefly, I believe that I was asked a question from Judge Trechsel, he gave me leave to answer, and of course there were no time limitations or structural limitations of my -- you know, it was a question on relevancy, I thought I was responsive. And as I recall, Judge Trechsel indicated that he found my explanation quite appropriate under the circumstances, so I don't see how that could be characterized as a speech. It was merely an invited response and I would like to call it, and if it was effective I apologise to the Prosecution but that's part of my job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Authentic interpretation of my words and sense. In fact, I agree exceptionally, because normally I am quite not entirely uncritical as you may have perhaps have noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Once or twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Here I found that the different topics brought under one umbrella of a thesis that the Defence holds made the whole phase really comprehensible and helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Trechsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And with that I just want to pick up on the last answer that you gave us, Mr. Perkovic, because you pointed out to two examples; if you recall there were two examples. And I just want to touch on that to make sure that I have it right. In the one example that you use you made reference to 1D 02058, and as I recall you looked at Article 5 and you said that this aspect, Article 5 of this document, which is from Siroki Brijeg municipality was not consistent with the previous statutory decision. And just for the record, I take it what you meant by that was the statutory decision on municipal executive authority, and in particular you're referring to Article 2 where it says that: "The municipal HVO shall consist of its president, heads of office, and other members who shall be appointed and dismissed by the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And that was what -- you were linking those two documents to show how this Siroki Brijeg they were passing this decision which was inconsistent with a statutory decision that had been passed by the HVO HZ HB; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. In this particular chapter there are other documents as well. I will not read the numbers into the record and will make a written submission for these documents to be introduced, hopefully they will. But needless to say, the remaining documents in this chapter, is it fair to say that not only that you looked at them but you were the one that arranged them in the order in which they are in this folder for your presentation here today, but due to time limitations of course I'm the one that's preventing you from discussing them. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I analysed all those documents and I did make this suggestion because I thought that this explanation would be simpler in light of all those who were present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Very well. And I -- for time limitation purposes I won't dwell on that, we'll move on to the next subject matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And again, Your Honours, we will be moving by way of a motion to get those documents in, keeping in mind my explanation to Judge Trechsel's questions on relevancy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, the next topic deals with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. We have a few documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. One short question, Witness. Earlier on we reviewed a number of documents related to the activities of municipalities, and you yourself stressed that at times municipalities would take initiatives that were not quite right from a legal point of view. You explained that these municipalities took those steps because the state was not present anymore and when there is no state anymore, when there aren't any state structures there, then it's up to the municipalities to deal as best as they can with the situation. Of course, that explanation of yours is quite interesting, and we'll consider it. But listening to you I wondered about the relationship existing between the HVO and the municipalities, and I was wondering whether Mr. Mate Boban, Mr. Prlic, and the others had the necessary authority to impose their point of view on the municipalities, whether we're talking about Topic, Kordic, or others. You yourself were on the ground, you were an actor of all these things, you took part in a number of meetings, you contributed to the drafting of a number of decrees, you knew everyone there. I'd like to know what you think about all this and "by all this" I mean the following: Did the HVO have sufficient authority to impose its point of view on the municipalities or can we talk at the time of a sort of dual system where you had on the one hand the HVO and on the other hand the municipalities? And balances needed to be struck between these two sides and sometimes it was the case and sometimes it was not the case. What are your comments about the relationship between the authorities of the HVO and the municipalities? In other words, were the municipalities always obeying the orders of Mate Boban and all the others or was it the case that the municipalities had some room for manoeuvre, they were in a position to take initiatives, because considering their own situation they believed that they needed to take more individual or particular steps as opposed to the central power represented by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If -- in an effort to reply to your question, I look at things both de jure and de facto. De jure the municipal HVOs were subordinate to the municipal, or rather, to the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna; and de jure there is a very clear chain of command or hierarchy that indicates that there is a possibility for the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to direct both functionally and normatively the operation of the municipal Croatian Defence Councils. De facto, and we have a number of cases and a lot of evidence to indicate, that the municipal Croatian Defence Councils did not operate in accordance with the regulations passed by the Croatian Defence Councils of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna where the Croatian Defence Council did not take measures, any measures, to rectify this situation. It is my belief that the HVO of the HZ HB did not take those measures for two reasons. In many cases, the reason was that there were no legal mechanisms in place to exert pressure or to monitor the situation, or rather, these mechanisms existed but were not implemented in practice and those mechanisms would have made it possible for the HVO to discipline the disobedient municipal HVOs so to speak. And the other fact, probably quite significant, is that the leaders of the municipal HVOs were in many cases members of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna and they were, as such, superior to the HVO. And the HVO did not have the political power precisely because the leaders of the municipal HVOs had the power to impose their decisions, their will, even if they knew -- even if it knew that in some cases it should have taken appropriate steps in order to ensure that the municipal HVOs should abide by the regulations of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. So let me remind you of the basic, fundamental decision indicating that the leaders of the municipal HVOs are also members of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Many of them also held high positions in the party, and the Croatian Defence Council did not have the political power to impose certain political solutions although legally speaking in accordance with the legislation that it passed it did have mechanisms that would enable it to affect the operation of the municipal HVOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Two points. I'm grateful to the President for having raised this issue. For one, I am not convinced of a rule that a single member of a higher organ, the Presidency here, as an individual and in his different function of head of a municipality can put himself above what is de facto the executive. I think that is jumping because the Presidency is a collective, and a decision of the Presidency certainly overrules a decision of the HVO but not the decision of a single member of the Presidency. Would you contradict me in that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I could not agree with you, in fact. A member of the Presidency of the HZ HB, just one of those members, was also Mr. Boban, for instance. And if we were to apply this logic, he as an individual could never have put a stop, could not have fought against decision passed by the HVO. And I'm not quite sure that that was the case. On the basis of my personal experience and everything that I know, I know that he and other members of the Presidency of the HZ HB definitely did have at that time this kind of political power so that the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not have the political power that would enable it to impose political solutions that were necessary on those HVOs. I'm not talking only about Mr. Boban. A number of highly influential people were there heading the municipal HVOs in Mostar, in Capljina, in Neum, in Livno, and so on, Busovaca, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I'll leave it at that. I find it still a bit confusing, though. The second question refers to the explanation given by Mr. Karnavas this morning towards the end, which I seem to recall as saying these documents were all relevant because they show that in the absence of a central government in Sarajevo or of a functioning government, the municipalities had, as it were, to take the law into their own hands to make their own law. Now, the example we had - and I'm referring back to pages 75, line 19 and following, and 76, especially lines 4 to 7 - it seems that here a municipality acted not in the perspective of any central Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina government, but they acted against the rules of the governmental structure of Herceg-Bosna. And that cannot be invoked, it seems to me, for the purpose of establishing what some of the other documents were invoked to establish. Could I -- did I make myself understood and could you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, I'll try to answer your question. We're talking about a group of documents that was discussed at the end of the morning session about the functioning of the municipal authorities in various municipalities, and I have to stress this in particular, those were passed more or less in the same period of time. So we're talking about the initial period from April 1992 through November 1992 or thereabouts. So this is the period when the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina. An analysis of these documents shows that in essence all of them deviate from the heading or the preamble that they referred to and from which they purportedly derive their legitimacy. In the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna the municipal authorities pass regulations that are in contravention of the regulations enacted by the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and in an almost identical manner the municipal authorities; for instance, in Tuzla enact regulations that are contrary to republican regulations, regulations enacted by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And this has led me to conclude that in effect because the circumstances were completely new, and they were the result of the war; and legal system of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not prepared to deal with them because the entire legal system that had to do with the defence, for instance, regulated this sphere of defence in the context of an external enemy and an aggression from the outside and the actual situation was completely different. So there were legal lacuna in the republic itself at the republican level. There were also some limitations within the constitution, the existing constitution of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so there was this huge legal vacuum. And because life had to go on and because some things could not brook any delay, the municipal authorities tried to regulate those areas in the best possible way as they saw it, taking as their starting point the real interest and the actual situation that they faced. So that's what I was taking about. Considering that the deviations from the republican regulations existed in -- throughout the area, and they were motivated by the need to regulate life in wartime circumstances. And that went for Tuzla and for Siroki Brijeg, for Sarajevo and for Livno alike, and that's what I was talking about in the context of the analysis of the documents that we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I understood that, but with the document 1D 02058, you have told us that it was contrary to regulations established by the HZ HB HVO. So here there was no lacuna, there was a rule, and the rule was established by the authorities of Herceg-Bosna. So why did they not comply with these rules? What is the justification? Do we have to assume that there was simply more or less chaos and many municipalities did whatever seemed appropriate to them without bothering about either Bosnia and Herzegovina or Herceg-Bosna normative texts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, by definition administration is inert and it resists radical changes, radical steps, it lies at the very essence of administration -- at least that's what my experience has been over the past 22 years. So there is this resistance, this inertia, in the administration, in particular in this case in the administration, the local administration, in Siroki Brijeg, in the municipality. Secondly, I assume that since Siroki Brijeg was not affected by the war directly, it was not at the front line, it was a municipality that was in the rear, away from the front line, the -- any arguments for the Municipal Assembly to stop functioning would be quite questionable and it was -- their guiding thought was that the municipality could function, that the representatives could get there and attend the sessions. They were not displaced because of the war. So it is my assumption, only my assumption, that they retained this solution with the Assembly appointing the municipal HVO and with the Assembly retaining the right to appoint and remove members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess I'm going to have to dwell on this a little bit, even though it's going to cost me some time. The first question was between Boban and the presidents of the municipality. Perhaps you can at least -- since you were there, you knew the personalities, maybe you can inform us with respect to some of these presidents and I don't -- we don't need to go into any specific names, you did mention various municipalities. How real was their actual power? You know, in light of the fact that they were sitting on the same body with Mate Boban, which you've indicated at one point was allowed to or took upon himself to have three different hats, you know, president of the party, president of the Presidency, and then, you know, the president of the -- of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And light of all that, what was the -- how powerful were these individuals, not as a collective but individually, within their own municipalities? That's number one.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, their power stemmed from two bases in my view. First was the position that they held, that was the president of the municipal HVO and the member of the Presidency of the HZ HB, and the second basis was the trust that Mr. Boban gave those people, the trust that he showed he had in them in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me be a little more concrete. Let's just say that the HVO HZ HB as a collective body was unhappy with a particular president of a municipality and wanted him removed. Under the regulation that we just saw, the statutory decision for the municipal HVO, it would appear that they would be able to simply pick up the phone, call the president of the municipality, and then dismiss him. How realistic is that? Because we're dealing with reality. It's one thing to be sitting at a desk, reading the papers, theorising, conceptualising, analysing; I'm talking about reality. Let these Judges know what was it like. What kind of power did the HVO have vis-a-vis the example I just gave you: Pick up the phone and dismiss a president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know for a fact that the HVO of the HZ HB did not like some of the presidents of the municipality and that was no secret, but nothing was done to dismiss those people. I assume that this was because of a realistic assessment that at that time, given the power those people had, it was simply impossible to do so. And in my view, I don't doubt for a moment that had the assessment been positive, in other words, had they assessed that it was possible to dismiss the president of the municipality of Capljina, I am sure that the HVO would have attempted to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. We'll move on to the next chapter, HR HB. We're moving in time somewhat. I want you to look at the first document, P 04560, P 04560. These are the minutes from the 50th Session of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, 27 August 1993. We see your name there and we see the agenda, and if we were to go, for instance, to item 1 -- I'm sorry, items 2, 3, and 4, we see that your name is on a working group; and you along with others, such as Mr. Zubak who will be testifying here, you were to draft the following pieces of legislation, a decision on constituting the Chamber of Deputies, Rules of Procedure of the Chamber of Deputies, and the fundamental decision in relation to establishing and proclaiming the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. You being there, could you please tell us a little bit about this particular meeting and why were you tasked along with Zubak and others to draft these legal instruments?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were entrusted with this task by the president of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. The explanation provided to us was that it was necessary to have this done because what was underway was the preparation of a new peace agreement, the so-called Owen-Stoltenberg Plan, which envisaged a union for Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state, a union of three republics, that is, of the Croatian, Serb, and Bosniak peoples. In the context of the realization of that plan and the preparations for the realization and adoption of that plan, it was necessary to carry out a transformation of the existing bodies and institutions of the HZ HB and also to change the fundamental decision by way of proclaiming and constituting the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, in light of that question and answer, if we look at the next document 1D 01778, we've seen this document before in this courtroom. This is titled: "Agreement regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina." First of all, do you recognise this document; and if so, what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, actually this is a proposal of this plan of the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan. When preparing these fundamental decisions that I spoke of a few moments ago, we had in our hands this particular agreement in the form of a brochure, a booklet, if I can put it that way. We had the opportunity of familiarizing ourselves with this document. Before we started writing the documents that were mentioned -- well, quite simply, in order to be consistent in terms of the proposals that are contained in this agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So if I understand you correctly -- well, let me back up. This particular agreement, do you know specifically who drafted it or how was it reached since it's an agreement, do you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me about the agreement in connection with Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right, right, that one, which you indicated you used as a basis for drafting the particular instruments in establishing that the republic -- the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were shown and we knew that this was the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina, that's how it was presented to us, and I assume that these people drafted it together with their associates through the process of talks with the warring factions in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, if we look at P 04611, we've seen this document again in this courtroom, it's titled: "Basic decision on establishing and proclaiming the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." In light of the previous two documents that we have seen, can you give us an explanation as to this one?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the fundamental decision on the establishment and proclamation of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and by that decision what used to be the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is transformed into the Croatian republic; and the provisions of this decision - to cut the long story short - regulate those basic issues that pertain to the constitution, or rather, constituting the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the issue of its sovereignty, the creation of a union with other republics within BH, the issue of the establishment of the government, and the capital, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And again, in light of your previous answers because I don't want to be accused of leading you, is it fair to conclude that this particular document, P 04611, was drafted so -- so as to -- based on the principles that are set out in the agreement regarding Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is 1D 01778? Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. It is my belief that this decision is consistent in relation to that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you look at 1D 0188 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Let us go back to the previous document, P 04611. It was a document that was published in the Official Gazette proclaiming the HR HB. Why in the preamble or in the reasons do we not find any mention of the fact that the discussions held in Geneva, the various plans including the latest plan, had led to the republic being proclaimed? Why do we not find any explicit reference to the international context? Because this was an ideal opportunity to give some kind of legality, as it were, to the creation of this republic towards a union of republics. Why do we not find any explicit reference to the position held by the international community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The position of the international community was interpreted in a certain way through the Owen-Stoltenberg Peace Plan. At the moment when this decision was prepared and passed, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan had not entered into force yet, or rather, it had not been adopted, it had just been discussed. So it was illogical for the preamble of the decision itself to invoke basically an international document, a peace plan, that hadn't entered into force yet. What was of particular importance for me as a person who after all did take part in the drafting of this decision was what is referred to in the preamble of this decision, particularly in paragraph 3 of the preamble where it says that the Croatian people, I'm paraphrasing now, is establishing its Croatian state community and is transferring part of these constituent rights to the future union of republics within Bosnia-Herzegovina. I think that in this way that was expressed, that is to say this decisiveness, this readiness, of the Croat side conditionally speaking to implement and accept this international peace plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you properly, we have to read between the lines. It was not mentioned explicitly, but in between the lines we see that this is in keeping with the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was the basic idea of the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. If I can put it this way, it was the most important part that offered a new internal set-up for Bosnia-Herzegovina. In the preamble we repeat in terms of substance that particular part, but we do not explicitly refer to the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan simply because the plan had not been adopted yet, or rather, hadn't entered into force yet. So legally it is illogical to invoke an international document that is not valid yet, that is not in force yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, following on my previous question, I had in mind the current recognition of Kosovo. I have not had an opportunity to read the constitution of Kosovo; and I was wondering whether in the current constitution of Kosovo there was no mention to the international community, it may be so, it may not, I don't know. But I thought you might have had an opportunity to involve the international community in the creation of this republic, and I failed to find in this statement at first glance anything that would lead me to conclude that this is a further step following all the previous negotiations without any explicit reference. But I do understand what you said. Very well. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't believe you will find anything in the Brcko district which came about as a result of the final award, I drafted that, and we specifically excluded putting any international instruments or mention of it. I mention only this because there are various ways of doing this and we can certainly bring in evidence regarding the Kosovo constitution, the Brcko district statute, and the statute of BiH as a result of the Dayton Peace Accords, which is annexed -- it's part of the annex to Dayton.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we go on to the next document, 1D 01880, this is a decision on constituting the Chamber of Deputies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; and, of course, we started off with the very first minutes of the meeting and you were on that working group. And here we see this is a decision on constituting the Chamber of Deputies. And Article 2 talks about: "Until the first free democratic elections, the representatives of the Croatian people in the Council of Municipalities of the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and members of the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be members of the Chamber of Deputies of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna." First of all, are you familiar with this document; and if so, could you please tell us. And secondly, in light of the fact that you were with the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna can you comment on Article 2, specifically where it makes reference to the first free democratic election. What are we referring to?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision is one that I am familiar with. This decision constitutes the parliament, if I can put it that way, the parliament of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna; and Article 2 envisages that members of that parliament shall be the representatives of the Council of Municipalities of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say people who at the first multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina were elected to this house of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]
