utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The first free elections, until the first free elections we know who the representatives will be, but when were the first free democratic elections to take place, if you know, and did they take place?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first free elections were held after the peace plan was adopted, regrettably not this one, there was a one-year delay; that is to say after the Dayton Peace Agreement was adopted. These people were representatives in the parliament of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna up until those first free elections that were held afterwards, after the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. And then finally 1D 02112, we see that this is a letter to the House of Representatives of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic, where he attaches six particular laws, draft laws, for review; and we see such as the law on organization and jurisdiction, a law on courts, law on public prosecution, and so on. Why was it necessary now to have all these new drafts in light of all the other previous drafting that you had been doing under the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because while the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna was still in existence, all these decrees and all these other enactments were of an ad hoc nature, that is to say a temporary nature. What was emphasized in every one of these documents was the fact that they were provisional. Now in this new situation, in this situation when a parliamentary body was coming into being, there was the possibility of dealing with things in a more serious way, in a better way, and to regulate certain matters systematically. Now the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, its president, submits these bills to the house for its view and its adoption. The point is that the nature of these regulations has changed; they were supposed to be of a lasting nature rather than of a provisional nature as had been the case in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at -- we're going to switch topics and we're on the second-to-last topic. This deals with the functioning of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and again this might give us at least a taste of what was going on at the time. 1D 02038, this is a decision on the election of the president, vice-president, and members of the government. Do you see this, sir? We don't see your name on it, but can you confirm that these individuals were serving in this capacity as is designated in this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that these persons held these positions. It is logical that my name is not there because I was not a member of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. I headed a professional body of the government; I was not a member of government.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to 1D 01873, we saw this document recently. This is a letter from Dr. Prlic to General Jean Cot, who is a commander of the UN peacekeeping forces; and, of course, in there he's discussing certain matters. Have you had a chance to look at this document and can you tell us or can you confirm whether in fact these activities were ongoing based on your personal knowledge and activities at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of this document. This was a letter that was sent to the commander of the peace forces of the UN for the former Yugoslavia, General Cot. On behalf of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna the prime minister expresses his readiness to fully contribute to providing security to the convoy of humanitarian aid and is referring to some other matters that are relevant in terms of improving living conditions in certain areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, we are not in possession of this document. We have a document which is completely different than which is numbered 1837 rather than 73.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We were just told there was a mistake, an error. There was an error in preparing the documents. We can put this on the ELMO. It's 1D 01837 -- 1873, 1873. If we can do it on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then while that's being pulled up or if you want to put it on the ELMO, either way, can you please -- can you please tell us whether you noticed a difference in the authority and ability for the government to function during the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna versus the period when it was the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, when we had Mate Boban, for instance, being sort of the all-powerful individual with all those different positions.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that to a considerable degree the influence and authority of the highest level of authority, which is now called the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, has been increased and this increase is due to the fact, in my view, that it got the legitimacy of the parliament of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna and once it was constituted, it enjoyed the support of the parliament of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: My colleague says on line 13 [sic] you said the highest level of executive authority, as opposed to simply authority. So we're speaking about line 23 on page 94, it's kind of difficult to find if you're not used to this but we're talking about the executive authority; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that we are talking about the executive organ of government, that is to say the organ that practically took over the functions or powers of the HV HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some follow-up questions, Witness, please. We did not have this document in the binders, but now we have it in e-court; and I can see the letter drafted in B/C/S and its translation into English. I'd like to hear what you think. I notice this; this is a letter signed by Mr. Prlic and the outgoing stamp is Bosnia and Herzegovina. We don't know whether we're talking about the republic or the country. And then we see HR HB government, office of the president, and then we see the actual stamp. We mentioned the stamps this morning, and here we have one stamp. Look at it, please. In it we can see Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina if you have a Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna? Do you have an explanation for this stamp here which does refer to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or is this a stamp that was used because there was no other stamp available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina for a simple reason, namely, the settlement on peace had not been reached yet and now the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna did not at any point in time bring into question the legitimacy of the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a state. At that point in time the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was still the official name of that state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're aware of this letter. As far as you know, did General Cot answer by way of a letter sent to Dr. Prlic, a letter that would say, Mr. President, further to your letter of 23rd of November, 1993, in which you asked for a meeting, et cetera, was there any answer or did the international community avoid answering in writing, in answering in letters where they would have had to mention HR HB? Was there an answer or not? It may be that you don't know but do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Mr. Cot replied to this letter. I don't have any information to that effect, whether he did or did not, so I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, you have affirmed that this letter in your view shows the enhanced, increased authority of the government of the HR HB. Could you be a bit more specific and point out exactly which element of the letter leads you to that finding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I spoke about the strength and position of the government. When I was asked by the Defence counsel to compare the authority of the HVO HZ HB and the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and comparing those two executive organs, I said that in my opinion the position of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was stronger. I did not link this strengthening of the position of the government in any way with this letter. But this letter in a way also shows that there is a new element here, this organ had much more latitude in terms of launching initiatives than was the case before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that. The counsel certainly linked these questions to this -- to this letter unless I misunderstood completely. But I -- for me that's it now, you can go on, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, perhaps there was a misunderstanding as far as linkage. I did -- there was a follow-up question, but it wasn't meant to be as a link.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Be that as it may, P 07000, here just -- again just as a sampling we see extract of minutes. We don't need to go through all of them through this in any great detail. I just want to point out that in going through them it would appear that on the agenda items 5, 9, 13, 17, 18, 19, I believe that we see you commenting or discussing, and I take it that was part of your function in your new position in the legislative office; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the position of this office changed. It used to be the Commission For Regulations, and now it became a body that was called the legislation office of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I guess this -- would this not be a representation of how the meetings were being held and the minutes -- how the minutes were kept and the dynamics within the minutes, within the meetings, particularly concerning the discussions on draft decrees or draft proposals?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unlike the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, now this procedure of passing legislation became much more complex. If you'll recall, I said that we had only one filter in place, that was the case before; and now the number of filters has increased and the responsibility of the legislation office increased commensurately. So that my responsibility as head of this office, because for every law we had to provide our opinion for the session of the government. In some cases a simple sentence would suffice. We would say that our opinion was positive, in other cases we perhaps had some remarks to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we look at the next document, 1D 01912, again this is a letter to Mr. Cot or General Cot signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic. It's 4 December 1993, and in light of the questions that came from Judge Trechsel and my comments as well or my questions -- now, if we could look at this letter, as I understand it you are familiar with it. Can you please tell us, are you familiar with the events that are being discussed in the letter; and can you link the events being discussed with the new executive authority of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The obvious intention was for the new government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna should try to deal with the problems in a much more efficient and decisive manner, the problems that had existed for a long time in the territory -- in the area of the HZ HB and HR HB in terms of organized crime, various offences. And in this letter, the president of the government on behalf of the government expresses his commitment that the bodies and institutions of the executive government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna should face these problems and solve them more efficiently, effectively, and with more determination than had been the case until then. And in this letter the steps that the government of the HR HB intends to take are also listed, and what I find to be quite important here is that in this document there is explicit and clear condemnation of the events that had affected the overall struggle of the Croatian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina quite adversely, such as the crime in Stupni Do, the destruction of the Old Bridge in Mostar, and so on. So this was one of the first documents where this is mentioned in those terms when there is this determined condemnation of all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01892, again this is just for representational purposes, this is a decree prohibiting property transactions in wartime and under direct threat of war. We've seen other documents when it was the Croatian community, this is now the Croatian republic. And under Article 1 it says: "Property transactions in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna are hereby prohibited ..." But if you look at number 2 and number 3 there seem to be some exceptions, one, with respect to relatives, first and second order, and then if there is a swap, an exchange, of property and we know that quite a bit of that happened even after the war. Were you involved in the drafting of this decree and what exactly -- why was it necessary to pass this decree if already you had laws on the books or decrees on the books that prohibited the transfer of property?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I participated in the drafting of this decision or decree, but there were no laws prohibiting this. There were laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina that made it possible to buy and sell real estate. We passed this decree in light of the overall situation in the country, and in the light of the fact that we knew that there were some attempts to exert pressure on the minorities in this area to sell their real estate for less money than they should have gotten. The purpose of this decree was to prevent any such attempt to exert pressure primarily on the people from the ethnic communities that were in the minority in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on anyone's part, and the -- so that this -- these people, or rather, that -- to prevent occasions where somebody would buy -- anyone would buy real estate from such people in a legal manner. And the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna was the only entity in that area that had in place this kind of legislation, to prevent any kind of abuse in terms of real estate trade that would be caused by violence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 01614 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question based on what you have just said. Here we have a decree prohibiting, for the reasons you set forth, sale of property because of the state of war. If I were to apply this text to the following situation, let us imagine we have a Muslim person who has a small property, be it in Mostar or elsewhere, and for some unknown reason this person has to leave the area where they live, will their property be guaranteed forever? Based on this text there will now be a sort of concealed expropriation or forced transfer of property because this document, as we see it, does prohibit, does it not, any sale, any property transfer during this war period? Do I interpret the text properly or not or is this the outcome or is the situation I've just depicted, does it result from the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under the law -- under the law on land registry books of Bosnia-Herzegovina that applied in the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna in its original form, no registration in the land registry offices could be done without the so-called clausura "lex tabulandi," which means that the previous owner had to make an explicit statement confirming that this real estate was sold or gifted or transferred to another person in any other way. This means in your example that this person, no matter where they -- where this person were, nobody could transfer the ownership of this real estate without that person's explicit approval for the transfer of ownership. Had this provision not been in place, we would probably have faced a situation that many members of ethnic minorities faced in Republika Srpska where because no such law was in place there were many transfers of ownership of real estate which were the result of acts of violence perpetrated against those people in order to pressure them into selling their real estate or giving it away. I -- it was our objective to prevent it, and I am not aware of any example, any case after the war in the territory of the Croatian -- in the area of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna where somebody would apply to the courts there for the return of their property because they had been forced to sell their property because of threats or pressure. So the situation after the war justified the existence of such a decree at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1D 01614, very briefly, I just need you to confirm, this is extract of minutes from the 14th session of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, 9 February 1994, and we do see on the very first page your name under legislative office and this would confirm, would it not, indeed this is the position that you held during that period? And, of course, we can see through the minutes that you occasionally make comments concerning various pieces of legislation that is being tabled for discussion.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that throughout that time I held that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. 1D 02113, and this is a letter from Dr. Jadranko Prlic, and it's an invitation to a working meeting and it's to the -- to a Dr. Vrljic, who is the Croatian Defence Council municipality of Mostar president, and of course we can see the various topics. Perhaps you can comment on that a little bit. Why would it be necessary to have working meetings with the HVO municipality of Mostar, number one? And number two, if you could also discuss a little bit the dynamics between the two, between -- you can go as far back as the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the HVO, and their relationship with the HVO municipality of Mostar as well as during this period, now we're into the Croatian Republic. Be -- and try to be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In response to your first question it is quite obvious that the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, and that's the president, were not happy with the security situation in Mostar; and for that reason they are -- they wanted this meeting with the municipal leaders in Mostar in order to find a solution to improve the security situation there. As regards the second question that you asked, the seat of the institutions of the Croatian Community, later Croatian Republic, of Herceg-Bosna was in Mostar and all those who worked in those institutions could see what the security situation in Mostar was like, as was quite natural. During the war unfortunately the security situation was not satisfactory for the most part, and I would say there was this continuous initiative and a series of meetings that took place during the war with the Croatian Defence Council in Mostar -- of Mostar in order to improve the circumstances, this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If we go on to the next document, 1D 01642, and this is a letter from the head of cabinet, Renata Sopta, wherein she's requesting permission for four individuals for movement during the curfew and one of them is Dr. Jadranko Prlic and, of course, by this point we all know he's the president of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, why is it that he would need to ask permission to the Mostar police administration in order to move about after curfew? After all, he is the president?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because this regulation bound all those who were moving about during the curfew to do so only with a lesse passe or the permission to do so, and nobody was exempt including the president of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're down to two documents before we get to our last topic essentially, and this is 1D 01955, and we can see in this document at the very top that these are notes from a meeting of representatives of the Bosniak, Muslim, people and the Croatian people held on 23 April 1994. And we see that you are one of the attendees. If you could just briefly tell us, what is this -- what meeting are we talking about? What took place and what was the purpose of it?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was the first official meeting a few days after the signing of the Washington Agreement which structured or put in place the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in order to implement the Washington Agreement it was necessary to hold a meeting and to agree on the initial steps that needed to be taken in order to prepare and to draft and enact the legislation of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina in order to pave the way for the first session of the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In this context at this meeting it was agreed, inter alia, to draft -- to prepare the drafts of the first laws of the Federation, such as the Law on the stamp, on the Official Gazette, on the organization and purview of administrative bodies, and Mr. Kasim Trnka and I headed two teams that were drafting those first federal pieces of legislation a few days after this meeting that was held on the 23rd of April, 1994, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The last document is 1D 00269. This is several days later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, very brief question, we've just seen in this document that there was a meeting of the Muslim side and of the Croatian side at a high level apparently because we see that Mr. Silajdzic is present, as well as Mr. Prlic, Mr. Akmadzic, you yourself are there. So obviously we are dealing here with a very high-level meeting, and as you explained before this meeting happened just after the Washington Agreement. How come Mr. Izetbegovic did not attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know. It's possible that he was not in the country. I don't know. I could only speculate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23rd of April, 1994, Mr. Boban at the time was still involved in politics or was -- had he been sidelined at this time, and we're talking about the 23rd of April, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that Mr. Boban was in a peculiar situation at that time. He had tendered his resignation or what amounted to that. He -- that's what he did, so in operational terms he no longer participated in this, he could no longer direct in any way those talks, those discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Karnavas, four hours and 53 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So based on the previous question and answer, you know, I'd like to think -- given the -- what we have seen and what you have testified to, there is de jure, there is de facto, and then there is what I would call de-Boban, that is whatever Boban wants to do can do, given the various hats that he had. As I understand your answers by this point neither de jure, de facto, nor de-Boban is Boban involved in the various events that are going on between the two sides. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Boban did not participate officially in this. I don't have any information, and I can't really tell you whether he contacted some of the people who did participate in all this, but officially he was not present or involved in any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The last document of this batch is 1D 00269. This is five days later or four days later or five, and this is a decision on the constitution of the Livno municipal council. And so perhaps we can look at Article 7, I thought this might be interesting to look at, because here we see in Article 7: "The Livno municipal HVO shall cease working on the day of passing this decision and the following shall consequently cease to be valid: Statutory decision on the temporary organization of the municipal authorities during the war or the imminent threat of war ..." So are we -- can we conclude from Article 7 that essentially the Livno municipality HVO ceases to exist based on this decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it ceased to exist in that form, and I think that this was how it was done in all the other municipalities. And this just goes to show how all those organs had been provisional in character. This was underlined in the decision on the establishment of the municipal HVOs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I only have a few moments left so the last topic essentially deals with Gabela, and, of course, on the 14th of July, 2008, we did provide some additional information to everyone, including the Bench and the Office of the Prosecution, concerning certain information that you had provided to us and that can be found in paragraph 3 of that letter. If the Bench doesn't have it, we can certainly make it available. So in light of that I wanted to ask you a few questions. First of all, let's look at P 07096, and this is from Mate Boban, this is dated 10 December 1993; and we see a decision on all detention centres in the territory of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna shall be closed unconditionally. Were you aware of this particular decision, a yes or no would suffice while I lay this foundation.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go on to the next document, and that's P 02679, this is a decision and of course it's dated 8 June 1993 signed by Dr. Jadranko Prlic; and this is to set up a county military prison. And then -- in conjunction with that I want to, because of time purposes, look at the next document P 02674, and this is for the appointment of a Boko Previsic from Capljina to head the military prison in Gabela, and again it's the same date. Now, my first question is: You having participated in the various drafting processes and attending the various meetings, do you recall these decisions ever being tabled and ever being discussed and concluded?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall those decisions having been discussed at any sessions of the Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or at any session of the Croatian -- of the government of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I'm going to go through the other documents and then I'll have a couple more questions. We then go to P 0729 -- 7279, and this of course is a -- it's dated 20 December 1993. We see that there is a meeting and these are minutes, and tabled under topic number 6, item number 6, talks about a draft decision to supersede decisions and we see the numbers, numbers 350, 349, and then 343. And if we look at -- so -- okay good. Can you tell us whether you were at that particular meeting if you recall?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I took part in this meeting, or rather, it is certain that I did, this meeting of the government held in Orasje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Then if we look at the last document P 07668 this is dated 22 December 1993; and it's a decision, as we can see, concerning the opening of the regional military prison. And I'm wondering whether you were present when this decision was rendered.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what government session dealt with this, but this is a decision on revoking those decisions, let me remind you of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember now, but it is a decision on revoking the previous decisions. I can't remember whether -- well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You're absolutely correct. I misspoke. Now, let's discuss this for a little bit. If we look at the previous two decisions it talks about that they go into effect when they're published in the Croatian community in the Official Gazette were they're published by the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. We can see that under Roman numeral II, and the decision P 02679 as well as P 02674. Do you know whether these were ever published in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was customary for all decisions adopted by the government to be submitted to the office for legislation, the one that I headed that is. And the office of legislation was duty-bound to send them to the Official Gazette of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I do not recall that the government of the HR HB ever submitted this decision to be published in the Official Gazette. When looking at the Official Gazette of that -- from that period, I noticed that this decision was not actually published.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you have any explanations -- I mean, you talk about it in or I mention what it is that you told me during our proofing session, but can you please explain to us what if anything you had heard concerning these particular documents. I'm most specifically interested in the document of opening of the facility.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle -- well, all decisions of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, or rather, the government of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in which it said basically that they would be published, they were actually submitted for publication; but except for this case I haven't been aware of any other such cases when such decisions were not published. I can only assume two things. First of all, that it had to do with absolute negligence on the part of the administration; and the second assumption is that, quite simply, at the time of publication of this document, at least in terms of what the heading says here, this decision did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did there come a time when you heard some things or you overheard a conversation or discussions concerning the drafting of the decision to close them down and what would it -- what was needed to be done prior to issuing such a decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended a legal debate, if we can call it that, a discussion perhaps which involved Mr. Buntic and Mr. Djidic as far as I can remember. What was discussed were these technical aspects involved in reaching a decision, that is to say that what was topical at that moment was the decision on closing down this centre and publishing that decision -- or perhaps some other centre, I can't remember exactly whether it was Gabela. But definitely the question was whether one can publish something that had not been published earlier on in the Official Gazette, and should this be put into the Official Gazette at all. The law was compared, namely, can we pass a law on abrogating a law if previously we did not publish what was entered into force? So that was the debate that took place in that context. In principle, it touched upon this issue as well, but I personally never had any direct knowledge on the fate of this decision that had to do with the direct opening of the centre, so therefore I do not have any personal knowledge in that sense, namely, whether and in what direction this decision had been made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, the Chamber's Legal Officer tells me that we have only seven minutes left on the tapes, and we'll need to have a break soon; and let me remind you that you've already used more than five hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Am I being told to sit down or am I being given seven minutes to run out the tape? I don't know. I just have one or two more questions for this and then I can stop. I don't have any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please try to ask your two or three questions very shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: As I understand from what you had told me and which I represented to everyone is the debate was: How can we close something down that hasn't -- that we -- how can we issue a decision closing something down if we haven't issued a decision opening it as opposed to publishing it -- publishing a decision? There is a distinction between what you're saying here today and what I believe you had told me during the proofing session. So which of the two?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall repeat what I said a few moments ago, I mean and what I said during that previous discussion --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I object to this question. He gave his evidence and now Mr. Karnavas is trying to get --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's the basis of the objection? Can I have a legal basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's a leading question and the evidence has already been given. He said it wasn't published in the gazette. He never mentioned the fact that the decision didn't exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have a document here that I presented to the parties. We have a testimony yesterday, we had problems with the translation; I'm entitled to get clarification to make sure that what he stated is either correct, what he told us just now, or whether what he told me back on 14 July 1998 [sic] is correct, but I do think there is a distinction to be made; and I'm asking in an open-ended fashion. Obviously this document was prepared based on his information. He has knowledge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So my question to you, sir, is could you be more specific or could you repeat your answer. Was it: How can we issue a decision that hasn't been published or how can we issue a decision to close a facility if there's no decision opening the facility? Which of the two? Try to be as specific as possible and concrete for the Court.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was discussed was that in the opinion of some of the participants in this debate it was not possible to publish the decision on closing down a facility if a previous decision establishing that facility had not been published in the Official Gazette. I personally did not share that view. I think that the centre could be closed down even without publishing these decisions, and that's what I said to you in my statement; that is to say, had someone asked me, I would have said that it was possible to make a decision on closing down the centre and publish it irrespective of whether the decision on opening the centre was published ever. Let me just repeat once again. I said that I do not know -- actually, we're talking about two decisions here. I do not know that the decision on opening the centre was ever submitted to my office, and I'm not aware of it ever being published in the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Karnavas. It's almost 4.00 p.m. we're going to have our first break, 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before giving the floor to the counsel of the other accused, let me tell you the following. I was told that next week because of another trial this courtroom will be needed in the afternoon for a video conference. Next week on Wednesday and Thursday we'll be sitting in the morning instead of in the afternoon, on Wednesday and Thursday in the morning. I'd like to now make a request to Mr. Karnavas but without any discussion, we don't have any time for this. The Trial Chamber made a decision about the guide-lines and paragraph 35. Mr. Karnavas sent us a confidential notification explaining that the Trial Chamber should or could request the Prlic Defence to submit a motion with respect to paragraph 35 within four to six weeks after the presentation of the Defence case. The Trial Chamber will rule on this matter, but before we make a decision we need to have figures, statistics, about the Prlic Defence. Mr. Karnavas, we need to know how many documents you consider tendering in writing? Are we talking about 50 documents? 100? 200? 1.000? 2.000? I understand that you may not be in a position to give us an answer today, but you may be able to do so tomorrow afternoon, to give us a ballpark figure. This is not a very urgent matter, but before we respond to your notification, the one we received on the 29th of August, very recently, we need to have that information. I'm not asking you to give me that figure now unless you have it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I can give you an approximation. In this light of the way we're presenting our case and our success in getting documents in or lack thereof about 1500, 1.500 documents we see. I have to read them. We're going to -- and this is one of the reasons, Your Honours, why we're asking to do it at the end, we want to be as judicious - if I could use that word, if I could be permitted to use that word - as possible, keeping in mind the evidence and what is there absolutely essential for you to have. We don't want to make -- just throw stuff at you, we want to make sure that we have reasons, explanations, as to why certain documents should be in, how it ties in. So essentially it helps the Trial Chamber and of course it helps the Prosecution, and they can take whatever position they wish to take, keeping in mind our case is much more condensed than theirs was. And of course as I indicated, they had to do with the municipalities and the topics and ours are intertwined, that's one of the problems, and we don't want to have to submit a series of motions. So anyway, we're at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I apologise. As counsel indicated, actually correctly, the Prosecution would like to take a position and maybe I misunderstood your initial comments. I had the impression the Trial Chamber might be considering a ruling without giving the Prosecution an opportunity to respond, and it is our intention to file a written submission in response to the application that's been made by the Defence. So we certainly intend to file a written response and would ask the Trial Chamber to consider that as part of its deliberations. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What we wanted to know is the figure, the number of documents, and now we know that we are talking about roughly 1500 documents. Let's proceed now. I'm going to ask D2 whether they have any questions as part of the cross-examination. Let me remind you that Mr. Karnavas used five hours. Theoretically, the Defence has two hours and 30 minutes, in other words, 30 minutes for each team but some teams may not have any questions. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour, yes, I will have some questions; however, we have an internal set-up of our own. So according to this line-up, it is the Praljak Defence that will go first today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of General Praljak will not have any questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I wish to greet all in the courtroom. We are going to have a few very brief questions for this witness in order to clarify certain matters that we believe have not been fully clarified during the direct examination today.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to put a few questions that pertain to minutes of sessions of the civilian HVO, and I would kindly ask the witness to interpret for us certain observations contained in these minutes. And then we are going to deal with the subject of civilian control over the military. My first question pertains to the document that was discussed the most during the direct examination, these are the minutes of the HVO session dated the 22nd of July, 1993, which is document number 1D 01672.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could Ms. Alaburic please adjust her microphone. We can barely hear her. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, please make sure that you turn the microphone towards yourself because the interpreters can't hear you properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did move to the middle position, believing that my colleagues would hear me properly, but I will try to speak up as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this is a document that we discussed today, Mr. Perkovic, we were interested in paragraph 3, stating that General Petkovic as Chief of Staff provided information about the security and military situation. You said that you attended that session?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if you know whether General Petkovic was invited to that session or did he perhaps come at his own initiative or did he simply happen to be there?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally did not participate ever in the technical preparations of sessions of the HVO; however, in view of the position of General Petkovic there is no doubt in my mind that the general had been invited to the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, His Honour Judge Antonetti asked you whether at this session the civilian HVO could, for instance, give certain instructions or orders to the Main Staff or to someone else in the military. This is page 33 of the transcript, today's transcript. Do you remember that question, Witness?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. In response to that question I said to the best of my recollection the session was attended by over 30 persons. This was -- well, a biggish room in that company. It wasn't a classical HVO session consisting only of the members of the HVO of the HZ HB; it was a bigger meeting at which information was requested about the military and security situation in the said area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Perkovic, is it a rule that when there are such broad meetings the civilian HVO, or later on the government, does not pass any decisions or resolutions?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part as far as I know there was such a rule, the government, or rather, the HVO of Herceg-Bosna, or rather, later on the government of the HR HB at its working sessions looked at bills and laws and items on the agenda of those sessions. There were cases, of course, when the government, or rather, the HVO would sit in this expanded fashion or, for example, with another body like the municipal HVO of Mostar and so on. However, then only specific questions would be dealt with, those that would be relevant to the HVO HZ HB and the representatives of the institution that is taking part in the work of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge to the effect that the regulations of Herceg-Bosna defined the type of decisions the civilian HVO or government can pass?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed that yesterday. In a document that we looked at yesterday it is stipulated that the HVO of Herceg-Bosna passes decrees, decisions, instructions, and decisions, I believe; I don't want to look at the document again now, so four different types of legal documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we go back to Judge Antonetti's question as to whether the civilian HVO or government could issue instructions or orders, may we conclude that this could not happen simply because the civilian HVO, or rather, the government was not authorised to make that decisions that would be called instructions and orders?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The civilian HVO, or rather, the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna did not, to the best of my knowledge and in my conviction, did not have the authority to pass decisions that would pertain to the operative use of the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we clarify this. When you say that are you referring to decisions that would imply ordering specific military operations on the part of specific military units, that is to say the civilian HVO, or rather, the government did not have the authority to pass decisions on engaging specific military units in order to carry out specific military operations?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You repeated just now what is written in the decree on armed forces. This has to do with commanding the armed forces. The question of commanding the armed forces of the HZ HB was not under the authority of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us now, apart from commanding specific military units in order to carry out a specific military operation, are there any other questions that are relevant and important for the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, and in a way these questions are contained in the scope of work and authority of the defence department at different levels, starting with the municipal departments up to the HZ HB. And in war conditions, that is to say when there is a war going on, there are certain defence tasks that are entrusted to the Ministry of the Interior, or rather, its departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Perkovic, the civilian HVO, or rather, the government did they have any kind of basic authority regarding the defence of the country?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course when we are discussing questions that have to do with finance, or rather, financing the war, that have to do with the defence budget, that have to do with all logistical matters, supplies for the military units, and so on, we have seen how many times the civilian HVO of HZ HB had on its agenda the question of mobilisation and so on and so forth. So these questions that have to do with the readiness of a community to defend itself and that have to do with these questions, that is to say replenishing the armed forces through mobilisation and logistical activities and so on and so forth, financing and so on and so forth; of course, inter alia, this was within the authority of the HVO through one of its departments, that is to say the department for defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we look now into this, whether this was the -- originally the authority of the government or the HZ HB or whether this was done through the departments of defence. Can we please look at document 00819, Article 9. Mr. Perkovic, can we agree that Article 9 deals with the powers of the Croatian Defence Council, whereas in Article 10 the authority of the defence department is being stipulated?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Articles 9 and 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Article 9 regarding the civilian HVO, and Article 10 regarding the defence department.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can agree with you. In Article 9 the authority and powers of the Croatian Defence Council are stipulated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that all the issues that pertain to the defence that you mentioned, mobilisation, financing, and so on, that we can say that these are the issues that in accordance with Article 9 of this decree were put in the jurisdiction of the civilian HVO and the government?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These activities are explicitly listed in this article. In my previous reply I mentioned just a few of them without making any reference to this article, but you can see here that these really are the matters that I spoke about, mobilisation, various kinds of regulations, financing, and so on and so forth. So this is what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I think that you have proven yourself to be an expert in the legal system of Herceg-Bosna, so could you please explain to the Judges and everyone else in the courtroom in the legal system in our countries, because I think that Croatia and BH are quite similar in this case, paragraph 8 in Article 9 what does it mean, that the Croatian -- the civilian Croatian Defence Council or the government shall undertake other measures necessary for successful defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In drafting regulations of this kind, it is practically impossible to exhaustively determine all the powers that may be of significance in any given situation in the context of the defence. In legal -- it is the usual legal practice to put in a general stipulation such as the one contained in paragraph 8, which provides that other measures necessary for successful defence can be undertaken. So the range of these measures can be different from, for instance, temporary confiscation of property, various machinery that is to be used for the purpose of defence; for instance, banning the military conscripts from leaving the territory, food rationing for the population or for the military if the circumstances dictate it. Quite simply, because it is impossible to explicitly state all the possibilities, the legislator in most cases introduces this kind of formulation, other tasks and so on, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we consider a correct interpretation whereby this provision means that all the measures that are necessary for a successful defence that are not within the jurisdiction of any other body of Herceg-Bosna are then in the jurisdiction of the HVO which must then take this measure for a successful defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, it is difficult for me to agree with this suggestion because the very subheading indicates that we're talking about the powers of the HVO but also of other administrative bodies of the HZ HB. And it is also indicated here and all the legal entities involved in the matters of defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Perkovic, we're talking about Article 9 here. Can we agree that in order to interpret a regulation it is not important to look at the chapter heading where an article is actually located?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a lawyer, I find it hard to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you trying to tell me, Mr. Perkovic, that Article 9 does not stipulate only the powers of the civilian HVO or the government, but also of the bodies of the administration of the HZ HB and legal entities involved in the matters of defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not only Article 9 that deals with that, it's the whole set of articles that are contained in this chapter.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I kindly ask you, can we please stick on Article 9?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: We're trying to determine what was within the powers of the civilian HVO or the government. Can we agree that Article 9 deals with the issues that are within the purview of the civilian HVO or the government?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other provisions in any other legislation pertaining to the defence to the effect that any other body of the HZ HB is authorised to take any such measures necessary for a successful defence?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decree in addition to the powers that it vests in the Croatian Defence Council, the civilian HVO as we call it here, also defines the duties of other bodies at lower levels regarding quite specific tasks they have in the sphere of the defence. To be quite specific, I'm talking about municipal HVOs and their defence departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Mr. Perkovic, I think that this is a very clear and easy legal issue and that we will all find our way around. Now I want to ask you about meetings from another session of the HVO, that's 1D --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'm sorry, Ms. Alaburic. I am not satisfied that this is so entirely clear. Mr. Perkovic, there is in Article 10 a paragraph, 24, which attributes to the defence department the powers to conduct "other business related to matters of defence unless the appropriate business has already been incorporated into the competencies of other administrative bodies." Now, to me this seems that it is also what at least in German terminology one would call a general clause like the number 8 that we have dealt with before. And my question is: Where is the limit between one and the other? In both articles it is said that in the first the HVO, in the second the defence department, is competent to take other measures if they are necessary or if they are related to matters of defence. I could imagine that this may lead to conflicts because both authorities may say, Well, look, here paragraph 8 or paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in connection with your question the difference in the operation of the defence department and the HVO in these issues stems from the difference in the powers between those two levels of government, the municipal HVOs and the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Let me give you an example. For instance, the issue of land registry or documents pertaining to that, that has to be kept in municipal -- in the municipality ex officio, that is within the jurisdiction of the municipality. That means that in wartime the defence departments in the municipalities have the power to, for instance, take measures to protect those registry books, land registry, marriages registry, and so on by moving them to a safer location. So this activity is not explicitly listed and there is a number of other activities that fall within the meaning of other measures that municipal bodies have to take in wartime. So there is a difference between the powers of the two, and they are based on -- they stem from the powers of the municipalities or the municipal HVOs and the HVO HZ HB. But we cannot rule out the possibility that in some cases there can be a conflict of interests. I think that we did see an example yesterday, for instance, there was a document stipulating that some piece of machinery must be mobilised, confiscated, for the purposes of war. The question is: Who has the power to do so, to confiscate this kind of machinery, for instance, a truck? And there were some cases where the interests clashed and powers clashed when the municipal authorities thought that this was within their competence and the organs of the HVO HZ HB thought it was within their competence that they were in power to do so. So we cannot rule out situations where there were conflicts, but this was supposed to delineate those powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, do Article 8 or Article 10 refer to municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 8 speaks about the records of military conscripts --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: 9 and 10, not 8. I'm sorry, this was -- I may have misspoken but I mean 9 and 10 of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Article 10 [sic] speaks about the powers of the Croatian Defence Council, whereas Article 10 speaks about the powers of the defence department, the defence department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Right --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're talking about defence departments, those departments existed at the level of the HZ HB, so this is the defence department of the HZ HB that is referred to here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. It is very delicate of your -- of you that you have also misspoken to make me feel less bad because you have two times referred to Article 10 and the first time you referred to Article 9. This articles seems to wish to escape us, but it cannot. Mr. Perkovic, I was referring to any conflicts not with municipalities but between, on the one hand, the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, which has regulation in Article 9 to which I had referred; and on the other hand the defence department which is mentioned in Article 10, letter (a), and both these have this general clause that they are competent in other matters. And my problem is: Where is the line between one and the other? Who determines -- how does one determine? How does one know whether a specific matter which lies outside numbers 1 to 7 of Article 9 or 1 to 23 of Article 10 belong to one or the other? It seems that both can claim competencies for one of those questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me try and give you a concrete answer when we're talking about these two articles. In Article 9, for instance, in paragraph 5 it is stipulated that the HVO shall issue regulations on the introduction and implementation of mobilisation. And when we're talking about the competencies of the defence department in Article 10 it is stipulated here that that department implements regulations. So if we compare the two, it is quite clear that the power to pass regulations is the one that the HVO has and it is quite clear that the defence department has the power to implement the regulations. So it is quite easy to see, to make this distinction, and to see whether one or the other went beyond their competencies, beyond their powers, and whether they violated those provisions on their powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I suggest that now we try and find an answer to Judge Trechsel's question together. If you look at the chapeau of Article 10 where it says the defence department, later on to become the Ministry of Defence, it says, "shall carry out professional tasks in the field of defence and protection," does that mean that when you have a provision that other unspecified tasks are to be carried out that those tasks are of administrative and professional nature and fall within the purview of the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree with this explanation. I think that the bodies the defence departments as administrative bodies perform administrative and professional tasks in the sphere of defence and protection.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that regulations in the republics of the former Yugoslavia were quite similar and that in principle there were no problems with the delineation of the authority between the government, the Ministry of Defence, and so on?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as a whole this decree on the armed forces is in a way a copy of the Law on All People's Defence that we were talking about, but terminology was changed where necessary and the ideological elements that were contained in the Law on All People's Defence were deleted; but in essence it was the same principle of operation and the powers of various organs involved in defence were almost identical to the ones that they had before the war broke out at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In this decree, Mr. Perkovic, the defence administrations are mentioned in Article 13 and also recruitment offices in article or defence offices in Article 14. So can we agree that there are three levels of administrative bodies listed here: Defence departments, defence administrations, and defence offices?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, we don't have to now look at the article, that the defence or recruitment offices performed tasks related to mobilisation; in other words, those were municipal organs entrusted with defence at that level?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in accordance with the decree, this was within the purview of the defence office, so I do agree with what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, could you please explain to us this: If the civilian HVO or the government at its session reaches a conclusion that pertains to mobilisation and if this conclusion has to be implemented, in terms of further decisions and the implementation thereof what happens?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, because it was quite apparent that the defence offices in some areas, in some municipalities, were not operating as they should have been, the HVO intervened by issuing relevant decisions that pertained to mobilisation. In most cases once such decisions were made a representative of or several representatives would go to that municipality and would first try to get into direct contact with various institutions to create a climate where the response to the call-up or to the mobilisation would be greater. In some cases it was the carrot that was applied, and in other cases it was the stick. But at any rate, the essence was to take various measures to ensure a greater response to the call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am interested in another situation too. What was the sequence of written decisions? If the HVO issued a decision on general mobilisation and then all the defence offices were supposed to be notified about this decision, what was the sequence of events from the reaching of this conclusion to a decision that actually reached a defence office somewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once a decision on mobilisation was made, the first logical step would be to notify the defence offices about this decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Okay. We want to know how they were notified. Was it possible to notify them in writing, in a document of some kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at any rate making the decision on mobilisation would entail a written document. Now, technically how this document was sent, this was done in various ways, by courier, maybe by fax, because I think it was possible to fax in that time. But in most cases it was couriered.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, if you know, this decision that was received by a defence office, was this document entitled a decision, was it a decision or did it bear any other name, order or something like that?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have an opportunity to look at those documents or to be -- I didn't find myself in those circumstances, so I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Then we're not going to deal with it any longer. Perhaps I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, I still have a question. You have told us, Mr. Perkovic, that the offices maybe not always worked well and then the HVO went to intervene; and I'm amazed that it's the HVO and not the department because they belong as can be seen from Article 12, paragraph 1, they are established within the defence department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you have in a municipality a response to mobilisation or a call-up that is 15 to 20 per cent, then the question of mobilisation of manpower in that municipality is not only a question pertaining to normative and technical finesse in terms of the implementation of that decision, it also turns into a political problem that exists in a certain parts of the area of the HZ HB. In that context, the HVO discussed several times ways in which the efficiency of mobilisation could be stepped-up in certain municipalities considering that problem to be a political and security problem as well for the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna as a whole, not only for the particular municipality to which that mobilisation pertained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, just one more question by way of a summary. To the best of your recollection, the civilian HVO in its programmes did it define that the defence of Herceg-Bosna was a priority issue and did they say that they would bow to that as a priority as well as the defence of the -- of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina too?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is contained basically in all the fundamental documents establishing the HZ HB and the HVO of the HZ HB. It is my deep conviction that had there not been a war and needs of defence there wouldn't have been an HVO either. That task is in the very foundation of all the institutions of Herceg-Bosna, including HVO which was one of the most important institutions if Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers, Mr. Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of Mr. Coric does not have any questions of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I'll turn back to Ms. Nozica then.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, before I start with my cross-examination I have an objection, but I would kindly ask that we move into private session for that objection to be voiced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Perkovic.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We've known each other for many, many years and there's no need for any kind of introduction. You have already understood that I would be putting questions to you on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Stojic. I will try to be as efficient as possible to a maximum. I believe that you've already had an opportunity to look at the pink binder I've prepared for you and you've seen these documents. I have not looked at any one of them earlier on -- I did not display them in this courtroom, that is. So what I wish to do is discuss something that you discussed rather extensively during the direct examination, that is to say the conduct of municipalities in the entire system of the HZ HB. For the purposes of my examination I'm going to focus on an important answer you gave, namely, that some municipalities at the very outset as soon as the aggression against this area started, they reacted as best they could. However, during the conflict some municipalities nevertheless did take upon themselves some obligations, or rather, some powers that they were not entitled to. So let us deal with this in the right order in terms of corroborating what you spoke of. Could we please look at the documents the way I have filed them. I am going to skip over those that are already exhibits, so 1D 0298, 1D 00298. Mr. Perkovic, this is a decision dated the 24th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, the first document I have here is 296.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, yes, we can go back to 296; my mistake, sorry about that. 1D 00296. That is a decision of the municipality of Livno, the first few decisions are decisions of the municipality of Livno, dated the 26th of October, 1993, and the decision is to approve payment of funds. We see here that funds are being approved here to the 2nd Company of the 6th Military Police Battalion. Did you know about this kind of thing, that certain municipalities through different kinds of aid that had been gathered are providing material assistance to the units that were in their own territory, like in this particular case?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did have some knowledge to the effect that in certain cases, specifically as far as Livno is concerned because I live there actually, I knew quite a few of these young men who were engaged; and I knew that from time to time not only municipalities but sometimes also wealthier citizens sponsored these young men by granting them certain financial resources for different purposes, cigarettes, pocket money, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, please let us focus here only on the organs of government in the municipality. I know that physical persons did this as well, but we're talking about the conduct of municipalities within the system of the HZ HB. So could you please look at the second document, and that's the one that I mistakenly mentioned first, that was 1D 00298. The document is also one of the Livno HVO, the 24th of September, 1993. What is being passed here is a decision on the professionalization of the army within the brigade Petar Kresimir IV. A few moments ago when you were answering the questions put to you by Ms. Alaburic and also over these past few days you demonstrated an enviable level of knowledge regarding HZ HB regulations. Do you think that this would be left to a municipal HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that this is in contravention of the normative acts of the HZ HB because the question of the professional status of soldiers of the HVO and the question of the professionalization of unit or a part of a unit was not in accordance with the regulations of the HZ HB within the jurisdiction of the municipal defence departments.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now skip the next document on the list because it's an exhibit, and I don't want to waste time, that's 2D 538; and I would like to ask you to look at 2D 01214. Again, it is a document originating from the Livno Croatian Defence Council. The date is the 18th of August, 1992. Could you please confirm, Mr. Perkovic, that as early as then the decree on the armed forces of the HZ HB, that it had already been passed by that time.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can recall it was the case, but this is one of the things that I mentioned before, indicating how difficult it was in the circumstances because it was impossible to communicate, roads were blocked and so on. It was impossible territory newly passed legislation, legislation that had been published in the Official Gazette -- I'm not sure whether it was published at all because it was the 18th of August, how difficult it was for this legislation to reach the municipalities that were relatively close such as, for instance, Livno. And this proves that this breakdown in communication was not only in the direction of Sarajevo, this is something that we've been talking about so much, but also the other way around, towards Livno and other municipalities that were part of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And in this context, of course the Croatian Defence Council passes a decision that in accordance with the decree on the armed forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna is not within its purview. It is within the purview of the defence department or the institutions of the defence at various levels in this chain.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. Now I would like to ask you to look at the next decision, again from Livno, that's 2D 01230. It is an order dated the 29th of December, 1992, so it's the end of 1992 and the order stipulates: "The order on the submission of the report on combat activities from the sectors of Livno front line." It seems quite obvious, but I would still like you to confirm whether a municipal HVO was empowered to pass such a decision?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The leader of the municipal HVO --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I've been told that a wrong document is on the ELMO. I would like to call up document 2D 01230. It's okay now.

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer was: Absolutely not. The heads of the municipal HVOs did not have the power to seek any reports about combat operations that the units of the HVO were involved in.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Let us complete this whole circle regarding Livno. Could you please look at the next document, that is 2D 01416. It is the decision, again of the Livno Croatian Defence Council. The date is the 18th of August, 1992, about temporary or permanent discharge, demobilisation, from HVO formations. Do you agree that this decision was not in line with the regulations that were already enacted by the HZ HB?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. It is in contravention of the decree on the armed forces of the HZ HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Perkovic, I deliberately showed you a number of these documents that pertain to the municipality of Livno because I heard from you that you knew what had been going on there because you had been visiting the area. But let us now go back to a document from the early times at the time when the defence against the aggressor was being organized up until the time in 1993 when this decision was made to professionalize the armed forces. Can we then agree that on the basis of this example that some municipalities systematically took upon themselves the powers of the HVO, meddled in the work of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZORAN PERKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. Ms. Nozica, what is the basis for the question? We have only seen documents pertaining to Livno, so I think the question must be limited to Livno unless you have documents for other municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yes, I do have documents about other municipalities.
